en: Oṃ tat sat. Salutations to Brahman.
This is the *Jaiminīyanyāyamālāvistara* composed by the venerable Mādhava.
At the commencement of all undertakings, [may] Vāgīśa and the other wise deities [be propitious].
I bow to that elephant-faced one, by bowing to whom one’s purpose is accomplished.

Knowing the reasoning that possesses valid proof, possessing firm resolve, discerning the specific distinctions within the divisions [of the system], having heard from authoritative sources, applying the rules of sequence, skilled in the application of logical arguments, possessing the excellence of praiseworthy analogical extension, holding the authority of constant intuition, free from all contradiction, the independent Lord, the illustrious King Bukkaṇa—whose conduct follows the context of the revealed scriptures—remains ever awake. 1.0.2.

That Brahman which is expounded as manifesting itself through the fivefold form (pañcamūrti)—in that [Brahman], the illustrious Bukkaṇa, lord of the earth, assumes the form of the Abode (sthitimūrti).
The sage Vidyātīrtha, shining as the form of Grace (anugrāhikāmūrti) within his own self, causes the omniscience of this [king], whose teeth are unbroken, to shine forth by means of his own virtues.

Just as Aṅgiras was the preceptor and minister of Indra, Sumati of Nala, Medhātithi of Śaibya, Dhaumya of the son of Dharma, Svaujas of King Vainya, Gautami of Nimi, and Arundhatī’s companion [Vasiṣṭha]— who possessed inward vision— was the preceptor and minister of the meritorious Rāma, so too was Mādhava the family preceptor and minister of that sovereign.
He, indeed, the life-sustainer of the wise and proficient in all scriptures, composed the weighty *Nyāyamālā* according to the system of Jaimini.
Having praised him in the midst of the assembly, King Vīraśrī Bukka commanded Mādhava, saying: "Do you expand this [work]."
Having obtained unimpeded grace from the four-faced lord Bhāratītīrtha Yatīndra, who was worthy [of such favor], he became like one of supreme excellence.
Having composed the *Jaiminīyanyāyamālā*, which bestows joy upon the learned, Mādhavācārya now explains it for the sake of those with immature intellects.

At the beginning of the *Nyāyamālā*, in order to indicate that this is his own work, he recites a verse containing his own seal (*svamudrā*) which expresses homage to the deity and is pregnant with manifold meanings:
"Vāgīśa and the other [gods], being well-disposed at the commencement of all undertakings..."
I bow to that elephant-faced one, by bowing to whom one’s purpose is fulfilled.

Having paid homage to the chosen deity, the author recollects the majesty residing in the Lord as Protector, for the sake of fulfilling the intended purpose: "He who knows the reasoning endowed with authority, who possesses firm resolve regarding distinctions, who partakes in the specific meaning, who has received the teachings from a reliable source, who is skilled in applying the sequence of methods, and whose excellence is enhanced by praiseworthy analogical extension..."

The illustrious Bukkaṇa, the lord of the earth, who possesses the authority for eternal manifestation, who is free from all obstruction, who is the independent Lord, and whose conduct accords with the scriptures and logical reasoning, remains ever awake. In this treatise on Dharma which is intended to be composed, there are the subjects to be expounded throughout the twelve chapters currently existing,
as well as the duties of kings (*rājadharmāḥ*) as declared in the science of polity (*nītiśāstra*).
All these qualities are found in this king.
Regarding the side of political strategy (*nītipakṣa*): there is *yukti*, which is *yoga* (union/alliance), and that *yukti* is accompanied by honor (*mānavatī*).
Pride and honor are the first of the four expedients—conciliation, sowing dissension, bribery, and punishment.
Sowing dissension in the enemy's mind is the second;
by these two, bribery and punishment are also implied.
By these four means, he specifically enjoys—that is, acquires—wealth (*artha*).
By this much, the destruction of enemies has been explained.

With what remains, the manner of protecting one's own kingdom is set forth: [the king] is skilled in deliberation and exclusion (*ūhāpoha*) regarding trustworthy persons, such as ministers and others, [knowing] that "this person is fit for such a task and not another."

He was skilled in employing the officials appointed over various villages by providing them with appropriate counsel, instructing them according to the following order: "These ascetics and venerable Brahmins are to be seated on the right side of the royal assembly, while these servants are to be seated on the left."
The prosperity of the entire realm, which is exceedingly vast as it extends to the very limits of the ocean, consists in the abundance of all things;
and this is praised by all living beings residing in foreign kingdoms, who think,
"This must be done."
The manifestation regarding what is to be done and what is not to be done—namely, "this is so" and "this is not"—is his constant prerogative, because this king’s intellect is everywhere unimpeded.
He is one by whom the affliction or obstacle to holy ascetics has been removed; thus, he is "one whose afflictions have departed.
Because other kings who rule over different regions are subordinate to him, he is not a servant to others and is therefore independent (*svatantra*).
This Lord is the embodiment of enjoyment (bhogamūrti) for the Lord of the World, Vidyātīrtha Muni;
he whose assembly possesses scriptural authority through discourses in the form of dialogues concerning the subject matter of the Vedas;

and whose life story also constantly possesses scriptural authority as it consists of meditation upon the secret meanings declared in the Vedas—he is this one whose discourses and life story are endowed with scripture.
Such was King Bukka: he remained perpetually vigilant, both inwardly in the meditation upon the Supreme Lord and outwardly in the protection of his subjects.

Just as he was skilled in the means of conciliation, sowing dissension, and so forth as taught in the treatises on statecraft (*nītiśāstra*), so too, by virtue of being an incarnation of the Omniscient One, he was proficient in the subject matter of the chapters on logic, beginning with the instruments of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and ending with the discussion of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), as set forth in the treatises on Dharma (*dharmaśāstra*).
And those meanings of the chapters will be demonstrated further below.

START MJaiNy 1,1.3 He demonstrates the omniscience of the King along with its logical justification: "That Brahman which is expounded as manifesting itself through the renown of five forms— therein, the illustrious Bukkaṇa, lord of the earth, assumes the form of stability."
The sage Vidyātīrtha, whose radiant form shines within that [Self], is the bestower of grace; therefore, through his own virtues, he shines as the joy of all beings, his station unassailable.

That Supreme Brahman which is perceived in all the Upaniṣads is itself manifested in the Śaiva Āgamas as five forms—namely Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta—for the sake of accomplishing the fivefold cosmic functions characterized by creation, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment, and grace.
It is explained that [the word *pratipādya*] means "to bring about renown" or "to manifest extensively.
In this regard, among those forms, this king assumes the form of stability (*sthitimūrti*).
Within that form, the shining Vidyātīrthamuni is said to be the form that bestows grace upon the entire world.
For this king is the Supreme Brahman spoken of in the Vedānta; for he is the abiding form of Maheśvara as described in the Āgamas;
and for the venerable Vidyātīrtha-muni shines forth, having become present within his very self.
Therefore, this king’s omniscience appears as an excellence beyond dispute even to the unlearned, women, and cowherds.
START MJaiNy 1.1.4:
By means of examples well-known from various Purāṇas, [the author] praises the minister of a king endowed with the aforementioned qualities for his capacity to act for the king's welfare:
Aṅgiras was the minister of Indra; Sumati, of Nala; Medhātithi, of Śaivya; Dhaumya, of the son of Dharma (Yudhiṣṭhira); Svaujas, of King Vainya; and Gautami, of Nimi.
Just as the inward-looking Arundhatī was the companion of the virtuous Rāma, so too was Mādhava the family preceptor and counselor of that sovereign.
In order to generate an excess of faith toward the work he intends to compose, he reveals the greatness of its author:
"The learned Mādhava, the protector of the Śruti, Smṛti, and the conduct of the virtuous..."
Having explained the Smārta [dharma] which pertains to all goals [and] to the twice-born, he now proceeds with the Śrauta [dharma].

The Smārta dharma—consisting of the commentary on the *Pārāśara-smṛti*, the essence of the Purāṇas, and so forth—was previously explained for the benefit of all social classes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*). Now, he has set out to explain the Śrauta dharma for the specific benefit of the twice-born.

Having commenced this work, [the author] first pays homage to the Supreme Lord— who bears the designation of the form of the Guru and who is the appropriate chosen deity here as the promulgator of all the Vedas and Śāstras— and then, for the sake of establishing the inclination of the listeners, he demonstrates the subject matter and the purpose. *Mīmāṃsājaiminīyanyāyamālāvistara* 1.1.6.
He announces his treatise:
"Having bowed to the Supreme Self in the form of Śrī Vidyātīrtha, the *Jaiminīyanyāyamālā* is here clearly summarized in verses. (MJaiNy 1.1.6)
The topics (adhikaraṇas) proclaimed by Jaimini, which determine the nature of Dharma, are the logical principles (nyāyas). These constitute the subject matter of this treatise.
Its purpose is the clear elucidation of these principles through a few verses that are easy to recite.
"The garland of reasoning is here compiled"—this is the formal proposition (pratijñā) preceded by the indication of the title of the work.
START MJaiNy 1.1.7–8:
He shows the nature of the work about to be composed: "One [section] illuminates the subject matter, the doubt, and the prima facie argument."
But another verse is generally stated by the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī).

The four constituent parts [of each section] are stated in a single verse in some places, while in others they are expressed through many verses; therefore, there is no prolixity. [Furthermore,] the subject matter (*viṣaya*) of each individual topical section (*adhikaraṇa*)...
Doubt, connection,
and the prima facie argument.
And the *siddhānta* (established conclusion); thus there are five members.
Among these, the *saṃgati* (connection) can be inferred by oneself for each topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) according to the method that will be explained immediately hereafter.
As for the remaining four members, there are in some places many verses that summarize them.
In some cases, by means of insertion (*āvāpa*) and deletion (*udvāpa*), the number ultimately results in two verses for each topical section (*adhikaraṇa*).
Therefore, one who fears [the resulting] multiplicity should not entertain the apprehension that the work will become too voluminous.
At this very point, clarifying the state of being the supreme among scriptures by means of a metaphorical identification (*rūpaka*), he demonstrates its ease of understanding:
"In every respect, the compendium does not exceed two thousand [verses]."
Thus, the ocean of Mīmāṃsā shall become for him a pleasure-pool.
Let the underlying principle (*nyāya*) be summarized by means of one verse, two verses, or several verses, as appropriate.
In any case, this work, which consists of a compendium of a thousand principles, will be completed in less than two thousand verses.
However, it does not exceed two thousand [verses].
Because of the great number and the profound depth of works such as the *Bhāṣya* and its *Ṭīkā*, the ocean of Mīmāṃsā was previously difficult to fathom.
By means of this present work, which is free from these two defects, it will become like a pond reaching only to the navel, fashioned for the play of young princes.
Although summary verses (*saṃgrahaśloka*) exist here and there in works such as the *Śāstradīpikā*, they are not present everywhere;

and even where they do exist, because the subject matter (*viṣaya*) and the doubt (*saṃśaya*) are not included therein, it is impossible to set forth an entire topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) by the mere recitation of the verse.
Therefore, one should not suspect that the meaning has already been established anywhere.
He explains the connection (*saṃgati*): "In the treatise (*śāstra*), in the chapter (*adhyāya*), and likewise in the section (*pāda*), the connections of logic (*nyāyasaṃgati*) are threefold."
Once the subject matter of the treatise and so forth has been understood, their respective connections should be inferred:
the connection with the treatise (*śāstra-saṃgati*) and the connection with the chapter (*adhyāya-saṃgati*).
And "conjunction with the feet" (pādasaṃgati)—thus conjunction is threefold.
And that [conjunction] can be inferred by oneself once the unique subject matter of the three, beginning with the treatise (śāstra), has been understood.
START MJaiNy 1.1.11-12:
He shows the unique subject matter of the treatise and its chapters: "Dharma is to be expounded by means of the twelve books; therein [it is treated] by means of the [twelve] topics (lakṣaṇas)."
The [six means of proof] are designated as: valid cognition, difference, subsidiary nature, application, order, and name.

Competence (*adhikāra*), extended application (*atideśa*)— both generally and specifically (*sāmānyena viśeṣataḥ*), modification (*ūha*), sublation (*bādha*), the common ritual framework (*tantra*), and incidental application (*prasaṅga*) have been taught in their proper order.
These are the characteristics of the chapters (*lakṣaṇāny adhyāyāḥ*).
The collection of the twelve characteristics is the "Twelve-Characteristics" (dvādaśalakṣaṇī).
The subject matter (*viṣaya*) of such a treatise endowed with the twelve characteristics is *dharma*.

The twelve categories (*padārtha*), beginning with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and ending with the incidental discussion (*prasaṅga*), are the subjects of the twelve chapters respectively.
In the first chapter, the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—consisting of injunctions (*vidhi*), explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and so forth—was defined.
In the second, the differentiation of ritual acts such as sacrifice (*yāga*) and gift-giving (*dāna*) was established.

In the third, the status of the *prayāja* offerings and others as subordinate elements (*śeṣa*) to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) was demonstrated by virtue of their being for the sake of those sacrifices.

In the fourth [book]—such as: "The performance of the *godohana* vessel is prompted by its being for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), and not by its being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*)," and so forth.
In the fifth—[topics such as] the necessity of the fixed order (*krama-niyati*) and its being subject to injunction (*vidheya*).
In the sixth [chapter], [the topics] such as "there is no entitlement for the blind and others to perform sacrifices" are treated.

In the seventh, there is general extended application (*atideśa*) based on both direct scriptural statements (*pratyakṣavacana*), such as "one should sacrifice with the Śyena," and inferred statements (*anumitavacana*) based on the names of rites such as the *Agnihotra*.

In the eighth [book], regarding the injunction “one should offer a *caru* to Sūrya,” the act of offering (*nirvāpa*) is indicated by the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) as having Sūrya as its deity; thus, by the mark (*liṅga*) of having a single deity and consisting of an herbal substance (*auṣadhadravyaka*), the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is specifically that of the *puroḍāśa* sacrifice to Agni, and not that of any other—such is the specific extended application (*viśeṣātideśa*).

In the ninth [book], regarding the mantra recited in the archetype (*prakṛti*) as “I offer what is pleasing to Agni” (*agnaye juṣṭaṃ nirvapāmi*), in the modified form (*vikṛti*), such as the *sauryacarū*, there is the removal of the word "Agni" and the insertion of the word "Sūrya," resulting in: “I offer what is pleasing to Sūrya” (*sūryāya juṣṭaṃ nirvapāmi*).
Such is "modification" (ūha) and so forth.

In the tenth [book], there is "sublation" (bādha), such as the omission of threshing—which is extended to the *kṛṣṇala* gold pieces by the general rule (*codaka*)—because it is impossible to remove the husks in their case.

In the eleventh [book], there is "tantra," wherein many principal rites, such as those dedicated to Agni, receive benefit from a single performance of an auxiliary rite, such as the *prayāja* offerings.

In the twelfth [topic]: the *prasaṅga* (extended application) occurs when an auxiliary such as the *prayāja*, performed for the benefit of the primary animal sacrifice, also provides benefit to the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) which is an auxiliary of that animal sacrifice, and so forth.
START MJaiNy 1.1.13: He shows the unique subject matter of the four sections (pādas): "Injunctions, explanatory passages (arthavāda), traditional law (smṛti), and names—thus it is fourfold."
The means of knowledge (māna) is declared by the four sections (pādas) contained in the first chapter.
In the first section, the means of knowledge in the form of injunction (vidhi) is declared;
in the second, that in the form of explanatory passage (arthavāda).
The explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) also indicates the mantra;
in the third [section], it is "in the form of tradition" (*smṛtirūpam*).
Tradition (*smṛti*) also indicates customary practice (*ācāra*).
In the fourth [section]—name-and-form, such as the variegated [body], etc., in both [cases].

The introduction, the means of distinguishing actions, the statement of exceptions thereto, and the distinction of performance— these are the topics belonging to the sections of the second chapter. (Mīmāṃsā-Jaiminīya-Nyāya-Mālā-Vistara 1.1.14)

In the first quarter (pāda) of the second chapter, an introductory discussion (upodghāta) relevant to the consideration of the distinction between ritual acts is described, beginning with the point that the verbal suffix alone conveys the *apūrva* (the unseen potency), as well as the existence of the *apūrva* itself.
In the second [quarter], the distinction between ritual acts is established through criteria such as the difference in verbal roots and the avoidance of redundancy.
In the third [section], there is the refutation of the authority for the distinction between rituals regarding the *rathantara* and other [sāmans].
In the fourth, there is the distinction between the obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*) performances. MJaiNyC_1,1.14 //

Direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and the cognitions arising from syntactical connection (*vākya*) and so forth; statements not made in reference to a specific context (*anārabhyokti*); those with multiple meanings; and those concerning ownership (*svāmyartha*)—these are the subjects of the eight chapters [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*].

In the first section (pāda) of the third chapter, among the means of proof such as direct statement (śruti), indicative mark (liṅga), and so forth, which indicate subsidiarity (śeṣatva), direct statement has been examined.
In the second, the indicative mark;
and in the third, syntactical connection (vākya), context (prakaraṇa), and the rest.

In the fourth [book]—the presence or absence of mutual contradiction among direct assertion (*śruti*) and the other means of proof, which serves as the basis for determining whether passages concerning the *nivīta*, *upavīta*, and so forth are explanatory (*arthavāda*) or injunctive (*vidhi*).
In the fifth—dispositional rites (*pratipattikarma*).
In the sixth—rites taught independently (*anārabhyādhīta*).
In the seventh [book]—the Prayājas and other rites that provide assistance primarily to many [subordinate elements];
in the eighth—the duties pertaining to the sacrificer (yājamāna). MJaiNyC_1,1.15 //

The agency of the primary [sacrifice], the non-agency of the subordinate, the consideration of the fruit, and the consideration of the secondary subsidiaries— these belong to the fourth [book]. (MJaiNy 1.1.16)

In the first quarter (pāda) of the fourth chapter, the status of being the motivator of the primary act is examined, starting with the discussion that curdled milk (*āmikṣā*), as the primary substance, is the motivator for the bringing of the curds. In the second [quarter], however, the status of being the motivator of non-primary acts is examined, such as how the removal of the calf (*vatsāpākaraṇa*), though non-primary, is the motivator for the cutting of the branch (*śākhācheda*).

In the third [quarter], there is an investigation into the existence or non-existence of results—such as hearing no evil verses (*apāpaśloka*)—arising from the use of *parṇa*-wood for the *juhū* ladle and other such items.
In the fourth [book]—the consideration of the dice-game and other such subsidiary elements belonging to the Rājasūya sacrifice.

The sequence [of words], its specific distinctions, increase and non-increase, and the relative strength of direct statement (*śruti*) and the other criteria— these are the topics belonging to the first quarter of the fifth chapter.
In the first quarter (pāda) of the fifth chapter, the order [of performance] is determined by means of direct scriptural statement (śruti), purpose (artha), textual sequence (pāṭha), and so forth.
In the second, specific orders such as the completion of each individual ritual detail across the seventeen animals belonging to the Vājapeya sacrifice are discussed.
In the third, increases such as the eleventh-fold repetition of the five fore-sacrifices (prayāja) and others through their recurrence are treated.
In [the section on] the *adābhya* and *citriṇī* cups, there is no recurrence [of the mantra], and so forth; thus, there is an absence of vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*).
In the fourth [section], there is the relative strength and weakness of the means of determining order, such as direct statement (*śruti*), purpose (*artha*), and textual sequence (*pāṭha*).
The qualified person, his duties, substitution, loss of purpose, initiation, and the sacrificial session (*sattra*); these [topics] are established in the sixth chapter. (MJaiNy 1.1.18)
In the first quarter (pāda) of the sixth chapter: the qualification for ritual action belongs to the agent;
it does not belong to the blind and so forth;
it belongs to women.
And by such statements as "he [should practice] together with his wife," the qualified practitioner (*adhikārī*) has been defined.
In the second [chapter], it is stated that for each of those qualified practitioners, the fruit is complete in its entirety.

The rules regarding the qualified performer have been stated, such as the restriction that there must be a single agent for the New and Full Moon sacrifices, and that a rite performed for a specific desire must be brought to completion.

In the third [chapter]— the determination that there is a substitute for a substance, but there is no substitute for the deities and so forth, the fires and so forth, or the qualified performer, and so on.

In the fourth [book], the loss of sacrificial materials is examined, such as: "If the *avatta* portion is destroyed, one should sacrifice with the remaining substance; if the *iḍā* portion of the clarified butter is destroyed, the remaining food should be taken," and so forth.
In the fifth [section]: due to a lapse in time, when the moon has risen, the *abhyudayeṣṭi* is the expiation;
for the *jyotiṣṭoma*, there are eleven initiations (*dīkṣā*), and for the *dvādaśāha*, there are twelve initiations.
Thus and so forth has been explained.
In the sixth [chapter]: "In that regard, the qualified practitioners (*adhikārin*) are indeed equal; the sacrificial session (*satra*) belongs to the Brahmin alone."
Such things as these were considered.
In the seventh [chapter]: "One's father and so forth should not be given away;
the great earth should not be given away."
Such is the consideration regarding what is to be given.
In the eighth [chapter]: the initiation-oblation (*upanayana-homa*) in the worldly fire (*laukika-agni*), and likewise the *sthapati-iṣṭi*.
Thus, the investigation concerning fire and so forth has been conducted.

The extension [of rules] based on direct statement is its supplement, as is the determination of the *sāman* chants; the two extensions based on name and characteristic marks belong to the first quarter of the seventh chapter.
In the first section (pāda) of the seventh chapter, the direct scriptural statement of extended application (*atideśa*) is considered, beginning with the words "The rest is the same as the Śyena.

In the second [section], the remainder of the aforementioned extended application is discussed, namely that by means of the word *rathantara*, which denotes the singing itself, it is the singing alone that is to be extended.
In the third [section], the extended application by means of the name *agnihotra* is treated.
In the fourth [section]: the extension by indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the extinguishing [of the fire], the medicinal herbs, the sacrificial materials, and so forth.

The specific rules of extended application (*atideśa*) found in the first quarter of the eighth chapter arise from clear indicative marks (*spaṣṭaliṅga*), as well as from unclear ones, from stronger exceptions (*apavāda*), and from specific [textual] indications.

In the first quarter (pāda) of the eighth chapter: "A specific extension [of ritual details] occurs through a clear indicative mark (liṅga). For example, in the case of the *saurya* oblation, there is the extension [of details] from the *caru* sacrifice, such as the act of pouring out (*nirvāpa*) and the designation of the deity by means of a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*)."
The state of having a single deity,
the fact that the substance consists of medicinal herbs,
and so forth, are clear indicative marks of Agni.
In the second case, however, there is an extension by means of indistinct indicative marks (*liṅga*).
For example, in the case of the *vājina* offering, the procedure for milk (*payas*) is extended by the general indicative mark of being an oblation (*havis*);
in that instance, the indicative mark is indistinct.
Because that cognition does not arise quickly.
In the third [case], there is extension by means of a powerful indicative mark (*liṅga*);
for example, in the case of the oblations (*havir*) dedicated to Agni, Viṣṇu, Sarasvatī, and Bṛhaspati in the *ābhicārika* rite, by means of the indicative mark consisting of the number three.

When the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the Āgneya and other sacrifices is reached in their respective order, the procedure of the third [sacrifice], the Āgnīṣomīya, is extended by way of analogy (*atideśa*) to the first, the Āgnāvaiṣṇava, on the basis of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of having two deities;
and this state of having two deities is more powerful [than the mere order].
Because it appears immediately upon the mere utterance of the word,
the sequence is weak due to its delayed perception.
In the fourth [case], the extended application (*atideśa*) is set aside in the case of ladle-oblations (*darvihoma*).
Now,

the commencement of *ūha*, the modification of *sāman*, and the modification of *mantra*— these are proclaimed in the four quarters (*pādas*) of the ninth chapter in connection with that [topic]. (MJaiNy 1.1.21)

In the first quarter (pāda) of the ninth chapter, there begins an inquiry into modification (ūha), preceded by an introductory discussion (upodghāta). In that context, the introductory discussion consists of such points as: the ritual duties (dharma) such as the fore-sacrifices (prayāja) are prompted by the transcendental result (apūrva); and in the case of the mantra for threshing and others, the specific nature of the rice or the fire is not intended to be expressed, but rather only their status as a particular means (sādhana-viśeṣatva) is intended.

The discussion concerning *ūha* (modification) begins with the observation that in the *vikṛtis* (modified sacrifices), there is no modification of the words *savitṛ*, *aśvin*, and *pūṣan*, whereas there is modification of the word *agni*, and so forth. In the second [section], the modification of the *Sāman* is treated along with its ancillary elements.
In the third [adhikaraṇa]—the modification of mantras;
in the fourth—the investigation arising from the occasion of mantra-modification. (MJaiNyC 1.1.21)

The omission of a door, its expansion, the unity of purpose, conjunction, the *graha* cups, the *sāman* chants, miscellaneous matters, and the meaning of the negative particle— these are the subjects contained in the eight quarters [of the first chapter].
In the first quarter (pāda) of the tenth chapter, the sublation of a means due to the disappearance of its purpose (dvāralopa) is examined.

For example: in the case of the injunction "The altar is self-made," there is a sublation of the preparatory acts such as digging and so forth, because the purpose consisting of the production of the altar has disappeared.
In the case of the gold pieces (kṛṣṇala), there is a sublation of the threshing because the purpose consisting of the removal of husks has disappeared.
In the second [section], there is an elaboration through many examples of the "omission of doors" (dvāralopa) which was stated in brief.
In the third, the cause of sublation is the unity of purpose (*kāryaikatva*).
For example: in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the purpose of the sacrificial fee consisting of cows, horses, and so forth, is the hiring of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij-parikraya*).
Likewise, in the *vikṛti* (modified sacrifice) called *bhū-nāman*, which is a one-day rite (*ekāha*), the same function belongs to the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consisting of a cow;
therefore, the sacrificial fees consisting of cows, goats, horses, and so forth, which are obtained through the rule of transfer (*codaka*) in the modified sacrifice, are set aside.
In the fourth [section]: the subsidiary oblations (*upahoma*) prescribed for the *nakṣatreṣṭi* are combined with the *nāriṣṭha* oblations obtained through the rule of transfer.
This and so forth constitute the collection [of examples].
In the fifth [case]: the drawing of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup pertains to the archetype;
and that must be drawn from the *āgrayaṇa* vessel alone.

The discussion concerning the cups (*graha*) and so forth, which arises from the context of sublation (*bādha*), occurs in the sixth [book]. The discussion concerning the *sāman* chants, such as "the *sāman* is to be sung on a triplet (*tṛca*)," which likewise arises from the context of sublation, occurs in the seventh [book].
In the seventh [book], regarding the limbs of the sacrificial animal (*paśu*), there is a distinction of oblations for each individual limb.
The entire animal is not the sacrificial offering;
the discussion concerning the *gṛhamedhīya* as an original (*apūrva*) rite and so forth constitutes a miscellaneous investigation arising from the context of sublation (*bādha*).
In the eighth [book], there is the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) expressed as "not in the *anuyāja*s."

The investigation into the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*)— such as "‘Not in the Soma [sacrifice]’ is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*), while ‘not in the Atirātra’ is a prohibition"— is useful for the purpose of sublation (*bādha*).

The introduction (*upodghāta*), as well as the *tantra* and *āvāpa*, the expansion of the *tantra*, and the expansion of the *āvāpa*— these constitute the four sections of the eleventh chapter. (Jaimini Sūtra 1.1.23)
In the first quarter (pāda) of the eleventh chapter, the introduction to the *tantra* is described;
in the second, *tantra* and *āvāpa* are briefly stated;
and in the third, *tantra* is elaborated upon with numerous examples.
In the fourth [section], the *avāpa* (insertion) is explained in the same manner.
Prasaṅga (extended application), the determination of the *tantra* (common element), and the treatment of combination (*samuccaya*) and option (*vikalpana*):
these are the subject matters of the twelve chapters; such is the summary of the contents of the chapters.

In the first pāda of the twelfth adhyāya, there is an investigation into such matters as the application (prasaṅga) of the ritual duties of the animal sacrifice to the animal-cake offering (paśupuroḍāśa), and the application of the Soma-altar (saumikavedi) to rites performed at a later time, and so forth.
In the second [case], the Savanīya animal sacrifice is the *tantra* (the primary ritual framework), but not the Savanīya sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*).
The modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) is the *tantrin* (that which possesses the framework).
The inquiry is whether the *anvārambhaṇīyā* (introductory rite) applies even to the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) and not only to the archetype (*prakṛti*), and so forth.
In the third [section]: the combination (*samuccaya*) of skin and clothing;
the combination of qualities pertaining to the wife, such as straightforwardness and evenness, and so forth, is stated primarily;
while the option (*vikalpa*) between barley and rice, and so forth, is stated as an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule of combination.
Thus, both [alternatives] were considered.

And in the fourth [section], both were considered: primarily, that there is an option (*vikalpa*) between the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses dedicated to Indra and Bṛhaspati, and so forth; and secondarily, as a subordinate point of the option, that there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā*, and so forth.

And in the fourth [chapter], both points were considered: primarily, that there is an option (*vikalpa*) between the two pairs of *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses dedicated to Indra and Bṛhaspati; and secondarily, as a subordinate point of the option, that there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā*.
Thus, the subjects to be explained have been summarized within the sixty sections (*pādas*) contained in the twelve chapters.
START MJaiNy 1.1.25:

Now, one might object: "Since many other topics besides those already mentioned as the subject matters of the various sections (pādas) are discussed within them, how are they included within those respective sections? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

One should infer further investigations according to their respective positions within the chapters, by means of introduction (*upodghāta*), refutation (*apavāda*), and through incidental (*prasaṅga*) and secondary incidental (*anuprasaṅga*) discussion.
Among the various subjects to be presented in the chapters as previously described, there may appropriately be some introductory matter (*upodghāta*).
Some is a refutation (apavāda), some is incidental (prasaṅgapatita),
and some is a further incidental consequence (anuprasaṅgapatita).
In this manner, the inclusion [of the word] within the *pāda* is to be inferred.
START MJaiNy 1.1.26:
Now, it may be objected: "Granted that the subjects of the chapters (adhyāyas) and the sections (pādas) are thus established; however, how is their sequence to be understood? To this, he says:
In this treatise, the sequential relationship of the chapters will be explained; however, we shall here briefly demonstrate that same [relationship] regarding the sections (pādas). [Objection:
There is completion within a single chapter.
At the commencement of another chapter,
the sequential relationship between those two chapters will be explained.
START MJaiNy 1.1.27:

When the relationship of priority and posteriority among the quarters (pādas) contained in the first chapter has been established, and since it can be inferred that this same relationship applies to the other quarters as well through that understanding, he provides an illustration of it: "Injunction is the direct means of knowing Dharma; its subsidiary is the speech of Arthavāda."

The portion of the text stating "Smṛti is rooted in the Veda" (vedamūlā smṛtiḥ) follows this sequence [in the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra]. Since it was promised that Dharma is the object of inquiry, and since the injunctive sentence (*vidhi-vākya*) is the direct means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), an investigation into it is appropriate in the first chapter (*pāda*). As for the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), its status as a means of valid knowledge arises through the mediation of the injunction; thus, it occurs immediately after the injunction. Because the Smṛti sentence derives its authority from being rooted in the Veda in the form of an injunction accompanied by an *arthavāda*, it occurs subsequent to the *arthavāda*.
Since a name constitutes a single part of a sentence, it follows that it occurs subsequent to the previously mentioned threefold investigation of sentences.
By this same principle, the mutual sequence of the sections (pādas) contained within the subsequent chapters is to be inferred.

Having thus determined the unique subject matter of the treatise, characterized by the specific sequence of its chapters and sections, [the author] demonstrates the fruit of that determination: "Having inferred the three types of connections as well as the intermediate connections..."
One should infer [the application of] objections, illustrations, counter-examples, and so forth.

When a topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) has been joined with the subject matter to be expounded in the treatise (*śāstra*) and elsewhere, that topical section possesses a connection with the treatise and a connection with the chapter (*adhyāya*).
And "connection with the subject matter" (*pādasaṃgati*); thus, three [types of connection] are formulated.

For example: in the second topic (*adhikaraṇa*) of the first quarter (*pāda*) of the first chapter, the absence of both definition and means of valid cognition for *dharma* was raised as the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), and its existence was subsequently established. That topic is connected to this treatise on the inquiry into *dharma* by virtue of its relation to *dharma*.
There is a connection with the first chapter because it consists of an investigation into the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

There is a connection with the first quarter (*pāda*) because the injunctive sentence is presented as a means of valid cognition. Just as these three connections have been inferred, [so too should others be understood].

Likewise, the mutual internal connection between the preceding and succeeding sections (*adhikaraṇa*) is to be inferred; and that [connection] is of many kinds— such as the connection by way of objection (*ākṣepasaṃgati*),
the connection by way of illustration (*dṛṣṭāntasaṃgati*), and so forth.
Connection by way of counter-example, connection by way of incidental discussion,
and connection by way of introduction.
And the connection with refutation (*apavāda*), and so forth, is of such a form.
START MJaiNy 1.1.28 He explains the application (*ūha*) of those connections, such as *ākṣepa* (objection) and so forth:
"Having observed the reasoning of the established conclusion (*siddhānta-yukti*) in the preceding system, [one applies it] to the subsequent system."
And one should apply the reasoning stated in the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), as well as the objections (*ākṣepa*) and so forth, to that [conclusion].

Having applied all of this, it is demonstrated as follows: In the first section (*adhikaraṇa*) of the first quarter (*pāda*) of the first chapter (*adhyāya*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that "the treatise concerning the investigation of Dharma is mandatory.
The reasoning for that is: "Because a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) is possible regarding Vedic study even when it is devoid of the desire for knowledge of its meaning."
In the second section, the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) is that "there is neither a definition nor a means of valid cognition for dharma.
The reasoning for this is: "because it is devoid of worldly forms and because perception and other means of knowledge do not apply to it."

The connection as an objection (*ākṣepasaṃgati*) is as follows: since, by that reasoning, Dharma is devoid of both definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), Dharma is equivalent to a human horn; therefore, the status of this treatise on its investigation as something to be enjoined (*vidheya*) is untenable.

Just as in the first section (*adhikaraṇa*) the status of the treatise on investigation as something to be enjoined was stated on the grounds that restrictive injunctions (*niyamavidhi*) are possible, so too in the second section, on the grounds that perception and other means do not apply because Dharma lacks a worldly form, it is established that Dharma has neither definition nor means of valid cognition; thus, there is a connection by way of an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭāntasaṃgati*).

Just as the reasoning stated previously is observed in the first *adhikaraṇa-siddhānta*, we do not see any such reasoning at all in the second *adhikaraṇa*; thus, there is a connection by way of a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa-saṅgati*).
These two connections—by way of example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and by way of counter-example—can be discerned everywhere even by those of dull intellect.

In the fifth section (*adhikaraṇa*), the authority of an injunctive sentence (*vidhi-vākya*) was described on the grounds of its independence. Since that sentence resides within the category of "word" (*śabda*) among the two categories of word and meaning (*śabda-artha*), the eternality of the word (*śabda-nityatva*) is discussed in the sixth section as a relevant digression (*prāsaṅgika-saṃgati*).

Furthermore, in the second section of the fourth quarter (*pāda*) of the seventh chapter, in order to teach the collection of Vedic subsidiaries (*aṅga-jāta*) in modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) such as the *Saurya*, the dependence of Dharma upon the Veda is established in the first section as being useful for that purpose.
This has been established.
Among those, the first section is the introduction (*upodghāta*).
Thus, this is the connection of the preceding section with the subsequent section by way of introduction.
In the first section of the third quarter of the first chapter, the authority of the *smṛti* texts concerning the Aṣṭakā and other rites was established.
In the second section, the previously established authority of the *smṛti* regarding the "entirety-encircling" (*sarvaveṣṭana*) is set aside;
this constitutes the connection of the exception (*apavāda*).
In this manner, the application [of this principle] should be inferred everywhere.
(First Section: The Declaration of the Commencement of the Treatise on Dharma) Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma. (Jaimini Sūtra 1.1.1)

Having thus explained the connections, and now desiring to grasp the four constituent parts— subject matter (*viṣaya*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), and final conclusion (*siddhānta*)— for each topical section (*adhikaraṇa*), [the author] sets forth the first topical section of the first quarter (*pāda*) of the first chapter according to the view of Bhaṭṭa:
"On account of the application of the injunction 'One's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) is to be studied'..."
The doubt is whether the treatise on deliberation (vicāra-śāstra) should not be commenced or whether it should indeed be commenced.

Since the cognition that [the Veda] is the cause of the knowledge of meaning is established by worldly convention—just as in the case of the *avaghāta* (threshing)—there is no restrictive factor [for this]; therefore, the undertaking of a separate [Vedic] injunction is not possible.
In this case, as in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice, there exists a restrictive factor regarding the *kratvapūrva* (the transcendental result of the rite);
since the scripture (*śāstra*) is the means for determining the meaning, let the exposition of the injunction (*vidhi*) now begin.

The collection of sūtras proclaimed by Jaimini, beginning with "Dharma is a purpose characterized by an injunction" (*codanālakṣaṇo 'rtho dharmaḥ*) and ending with "And because it is seen in the case of the *anvāhārya*," constitutes the treatise for the investigation of Dharma.
Regarding this first section (*adhikaraṇa*), some maintain that the injunction to study—"The Veda is to be studied"—culminates merely in the grasping of the syllables.
Others, however, say: "This study is enjoined for the sake of a visible purpose, which is the knowledge of the meaning;
and such knowledge of the meaning is not possible without inquiry."
"Then [it follows that] injunction is the motivator for the treatise of inquiry.
Regarding this, there arises the following doubt: "Is this treatise of inquiry not to be commenced because it is motivated by an injunction, or is it to be commenced?"

In this regard, the proponent who asserts that "the injunction for study is for the sake of knowing the meaning" must be asked: is study, which was absolutely unestablished (*atyantāprāpta*), being enjoined, or is it being restricted (*niyamyate*) as something only partially unestablished (*pakṣe 'prāpta*), like the threshing of grain?
It cannot be the first case; for [it would follow that] the Vedic study under dispute is not the cause of knowing the meaning.
Because it is a study,
like the study of the Mahābhārata;
for by this very inference, independent of any injunction, [the duty] is already established.
Let it be, then, the second position;
for it is possible that this is an injunction of restriction (*niyamavidhi*), just like the threshing of grain.

Just as threshing—since rice can be produced either by threshing or by scratching with the fingernails—is not necessarily established in every case, and is thus restricted by an injunction such that it must certainly be performed; so too here.

If it is argued that, since knowledge of the meaning can arise through reading from a written text or through study preceded by a teacher, the study that might otherwise not be undertaken is enjoined by the injunction as an alternative, we say no;
for there is a disparity.

It is only by means of rice grains produced through threshing (*avaghāta*)—acting through the intermediate *apūrva*—that the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) produce the ultimate *apūrva*, and not otherwise.
Therefore, while the unseen potency (*apūrva*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices serves as the basis for the restrictive rule (*niyama*) regarding threshing,

in this case, since the performance of the sacrifice is accomplished by the knowledge of the meaning derived solely from the written text, there is no basis for a restrictive rule regarding Vedic study.

Consequently, because neither of the two types of injunctions is possible, the commencement of the science of inquiry (*mīmāṃsā*) as a means to the knowledge of the meaning is not mandatory (*vaidha*).
If it is asked, "In that case, what is the fate of the injunction being heard?

we reply: the object to be enjoined is merely the acquisition of syllables for the sake of heaven. Although heaven is not explicitly mentioned, it must be inferred according to the principle of the Viśvajit sacrifice.

By the sūtra, "That [sacrifice] would have heaven as its result, because there is no distinction with respect to all [people]" (Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 4.3.15), the qualification of the fruit as heaven was established through reasoning in order to determine an eligible performer even though it was not explicitly mentioned in the case of the Viśvajit sacrifice. Let it be the same for the study [of the Veda] as well.
With this very point in mind, it has been said:
"Since the desired result is obtained even without an injunction, the injunction does not have that [result] as its purpose;
rather, heaven must be postulated through the power of the injunction, as in the case of the Viśvajit sacrifice and others."
This being the case, the scriptural injunction, "Having studied the Veda, one should perform the ceremonial bath (snāna)," is upheld;
for in this scripture, the immediate succession between the study of the Veda and its repetition is understood.
According to your view, however, even after the Veda has been studied, one must continue to reside in the teacher's house for the purpose of investigating dharma.
That being the case, its status as an internal part [of the Veda] is not sublated.

Therefore, since the treatise on inquiry lacks the character of a mandatory injunction (*vaidhatva*), and since dharma is established by mere recitation and because of the scriptural rule for the *samāvartana* (the student's return home), it follows that the treatise on the inquiry into dharma need not be commenced; such is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
To this, it is replied: as for what was stated—that "because it is already established in the world, there is no injunction for what is unattained"—[that is incorrect].
Let it be so;
however, its status as a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) cannot be denied.

Just as the supreme transcendental result (*paramāpūrva*) produced by the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) cannot have its status as a restrictive injunction denied when it is not explicitly stated.

Just as the supreme *apūrva* produced by the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices will be the postulator (*kalpaka*) of the intermediate *apūrva* produced by the restriction of the *avaghāta* (threshing), so too,
if the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the restriction were not admitted, the injunction being heard would be purposeless.
Nor is it appropriate to hold that its purpose is heaven according to the *Viśvajit* principle.
Since a result with visible fruit is possible through knowledge of the object, it is impossible to postulate an unseen [result];
therefore it has been said:
"When a visible fruit is being obtained, there is no postulation of an unseen one."
"But since the injunction serves the purpose of restriction, it will not be meaningless. Thus [it is said].

If it is argued that even so, since a person who has studied the Vedas and mastered the auxiliary sciences such as grammar can still attain knowledge of their meaning, the treatise on inquiry (*vicāra-śāstra*) would be useless—this is not so;
for although mere knowledge may be possible, definitive certainty (*nirṇaya*) depends upon inquiry.
As in the case of the injunction, "One places the sugar-lumps smeared [with something]," [the doubt arises whether they are smeared with] "clarified butter alone,"...
This conclusion—that [clarified butter] is not [to be used] with oil and so forth—is not established by grammar, etymology, or traditional exegesis;
rather, the science of inquiry (mīmāṃsā) will determine the meaning from the supplementary statement, "Clarified butter is indeed light. Therefore, inquiry is enjoined by scripture.

The scriptural injunction, "Having studied the Veda, one should perform the ceremonial bath (*snāna*)," teaches only the sequential order and the identity of the agent between the study and the graduation ceremony,
but not immediate succession.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the scripture of inquiry must be commenced precisely by virtue of this injunction.
In this very section, he states the opinion of the Guru (Bhartṛmitra): "Alternatively, since [the purpose of study] is established through teaching, there is no injunction regarding study."
Therefore, the preceding and following positions must be established by means of other reasons.

If it is argued that teaching can be accomplished even for a child who lacks an understanding of the meaning, then the scripture would be rendered devoid of subject matter and fruitless; therefore, let it be disregarded.

Since the understanding of the meaning [of the Veda] is obtained by oneself, and since there is no removal of the desire to speak [it], the subject matter and other requirements are easily accomplished; therefore, the treatise (śāstra) is commenced. [Manu Smṛti 2.36:
"One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa at eight years of age..."
The injunction "one should teach him" prescribes the act of teaching; nor is there an absence of a person to be enjoined here,
because one who desires the status of a teacher is the one to be enjoined.

By the word "upanayīta" (one should initiate), through the ātmanepada ending prescribed by Pāṇini’s sūtra "saṃmānanotsañjanācāryakaraṇajñānabhṛtivigaṇanavyayeṣu niyaḥ" (Pā. Sū. 1.3.36) regarding the act of making someone an Ācārya, the status of being an Ācārya is understood as a qualification of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*). That is, the one who is to be enjoined in the act of initiation.
The same applies to teaching as well, because the two have a single purpose.

This being so, since teaching performed by the teacher cannot be accomplished without the recitation performed by the student, the performance of recitation is established simply through the injunction regarding teaching; therefore, a separate injunction [for recitation] need not be accepted.
The injunctive statement being heard is also logically consistent as a permanent restatement (nityānuvāda).
Therefore, having relied upon the injunction for study, the prima facie and final positions previously set forth must be described in another way.
However, there is no disagreement regarding the subject matter or the doubt.
The subject matter is the science of inquiry (*vicāraśāstra*).
The doubt is whether it is non-scriptural (*avaidha*) or scriptural (*vaidha*).

In this regard, the proponent of its scriptural status should be asked: does the instruction performed by the teacher—which is itself enjoined—induce the student’s comprehension of the meaning as well, or is it merely the recitation of the text?
Not the first [alternative],
because teaching is accomplished even without the knowledge of the meaning;
for the mere recitation of the text does not constitute an object of inquiry.
The subject matter (*viṣaya*) is an object understood at first glance but which remains doubtful.
This being so, what need is there to mention doubt where there is no comprehension of the object at all?
Ascertainment (*nirṇaya*) is the fruit of inquiry (*vicāra*).
That [purpose] too is as far removed as the objects [of the senses].
Therefore, since there is no purpose regarding the objects, the treatise of inquiry should not be undertaken; such is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
To this it is replied: "Let it be that the comprehension of meaning is not employed for the sake of teaching."

Nevertheless, for one who has studied the Veda with its auxiliary sciences (vedāṅgas) and is proficient in grammar, etymology, and philology, the comprehension of the meaning occurs spontaneously even in the case of the Veda, just as it does in human-authored texts.

If it is argued that—just as in the case of "Eat poison," where the literal meaning, though perceived, is not intended—the absence of a subject matter and so forth regarding the Vedic meaning remains the same; we say no.
Because it is impossible for there to be no intention to speak;
and because the literal meaning of the statement regarding eating poison was abandoned so that there might be no contradiction with its being composed by a trustworthy person (*āpta*),
why is it not the case that the Veda possesses an intended meaning?

And regarding the meaning of the Veda intended to be expressed, whatever doubt a person may have, all of that is the subject matter of the science of inquiry (*vicāra-śāstra*). The determination thereof is its purpose.
Therefore, since the meaning being understood through the study prompted by the injunction to teach must be investigated, it is established that the science of inquiry is mandatory (*vaidhatva*).
(Second Section: On the Characteristics of Dharma) [Sūtra: Dharma is a beneficial purpose characterized by Vedic injunction. Jaimini 1.1.2.

He sets forth the second section according to the opinion of Bhaṭṭa: "Dharma, which is the subject of inquiry, is considered to be either devoid of definition or endowed with it; likewise, it is considered to be either devoid of means of knowledge or endowed with them. (MJaiNy 1.1.35)
What indeed could be the characteristic of that which is devoid of worldly forms?
Any suspicion of pride is far removed from it, because perception and the other means of knowledge do not operate there.
Indeed, the form of an injunction (*codanā*) is the defining characteristic when it possesses [the capacity for] meaning;
for this very reason, the injunction alone is our means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in this matter—why [should it not be so]?
For the establishment of an entity occurs through both its defining characteristic and its means of valid cognition.
Therefore they say:
"The establishment of the object of knowledge depends upon the means of knowledge, and the establishment of the means of knowledge depends upon its definition.
A definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is a certain form, well-known in the world, residing in the thing to be defined (*lakṣya*), which distinguishes it from things of the same and different classes.

When, through that definition (*lakṣaṇa*), a cognition of possibility regarding the object to be defined (*lakṣya*) has arisen, one who is intent on knowing it perceives it by means of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

For example, having heard the statement, "A cow is that which possesses a dewlap and so forth," one searches among four-footed living beings for the object characterized by those marks and perceives with the eye, "This is a cow.
Since this is the case, because Dharma is not of this world (*alaukika*), it has no definition.

In that case, why would there be an effort to cognize it? Even if it were somehow applicable, the presence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) therein cannot even be suspected. To begin with, perception (*pratyakṣa*) does not operate here.
Because dharma is devoid of form and other such qualities, there is no apprehension of pervasion (vyāpti); therefore, there is no inference.
Furthermore, the apprehension of the relationship (saṃgati) of words is rooted in perception and the like, as well as in inference.
Consequently, because there is no linguistic derivation [of its nature], even scripture (*āgama*) does not apply to it.

Thus, when it is argued that dharma is devoid of both defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), we reply: although the worldly form accessible through the eyes and other senses may be absent, nevertheless, there exists a form accessible through scriptural injunction (*codanā*), characterized by such things as being the means for achieving the fruit of heaven.
Thus, the definition is: "Dharma is that which, being a beneficial purpose (*artha*), is accessible through Vedic injunction (*codanā*).

If it were stated simply that "Dharma is a beneficial purpose," there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to Brahman, to acts such as bowing to a shrine (*caityavandana*), and to objects such as a jar.
To exclude these, it is specified that it must be "accessible through Vedic injunction."

If only that much were stated—namely, "that which is to be understood through injunction"—there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to rituals of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) such as the *śyena*, which, though enjoined, result in undesirable consequences and are thus of the nature of harm.
To exclude those, the word "beneficial" (*artha*) was stated.
Even though the fruit of the *śyena* sacrifice is the killing of an enemy, [it is nevertheless considered beneficial for the sacrificer].
It is not that hell itself is the hawk;
nevertheless, because that killing is a cause for hell, the hawk is an evil through the medium of that killing.
Nor should it be suspected that, by this logic, the injury to the animal in the Agniṣomīya sacrifice would also be a cause for hell on account of being a "killing."
Since that [action] is an auxiliary element of the sacrifice (*kratvaṅga*), there is no result other than the heaven that is the fruit of the sacrifice;
for when something is cognizable through an injunction (*codanā*), its status as an object of human purpose (*arthatva*) constitutes the definition of *dharma*.
Therefore, with respect to *dharma*, the injunctive statement (*vidhivākya*) which makes it known is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Although *dharma* is not an object of perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*),
nevertheless, its understanding is possible through the co-occurrence with well-known words.
Therefore, *dharma* is established by means of both definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
In this very section (adhikaraṇa), [Śaṅkara] states the most important point: "Alternatively, is the meaning of the Vedas to be known through the mantras and so forth?"
Furthermore, even the Accomplished One (Siddhārtha) is either to be understood solely through injunctions, or he is merely the object of the action to be performed.

In the case of words such as *go* and *gāvī*, there is no restriction whatsoever regarding their correctness or their usage;

"One should employ only correct forms; only words such as *go* (cow) and the like are correct"—this is the restrictive rule based on the successive tradition of grammatical analysis. Those proficient in grammar employ this word "cow" (*go*) with respect to an object possessing a dewlap and other such characteristics.
However, by those who are ignorant of that [correct word], following their own respective regional dialects, [they use] *gāvī*, *goṇī*, *gopotalikā*, and so forth.
Words such as these are employed;
however, in that regard, there is no restrictive rule to determine that "only such a word is correct, not such another."
Likewise, even in the case of yoga, that [restriction] does not exist: the usage of elders is not a regulator in the sense that "only such a word should be employed,
not such another," because that [usage] is common to all words.
Nor is the grammatical tradition (vyākaraṇasmṛti) restrictive,
because it lacks a foundation and is therefore not a valid authority;
for its foundation is not the usage of experts.
Because it would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*):
the establishment of the authority of the grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*) depends on the establishment of the expertise of those who employ [the words] in accordance with it;
and the establishment of that [expertise] depends on the authority of grammar, which is rooted in their usage.
Therefore, since there is no fixed rule regarding the use of correct words, this being the position reached,
we reply: there is indeed a rule that "one should employ only correct words, and not corrupt ones."
This is because one hears two Vedic statements—one expressing a fault and the other expressing a merit—respectively in both cases.
The statement expressing a merit is: "A single word, correctly understood and properly employed, becomes a cow of plenty that fulfills all desires in the heavenly world.
The statement expressing a fault is: "Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa should not speak like a barbarian, nor should he speak incorrectly."
"A corrupt word is indeed a barbarian"—this is the statement regarding the fault.
Just as there is a restriction regarding usage, so too must a restriction regarding correctness be understood: "Only *go* and the like are correct, but not *gāvī* and the like."
In this matter, grammar serves as the regulating authority;
nor is it rootless, for each preceding grammar serves as the basis for the subsequent one.

Intending this very point, it has been said: "In that regard, there is no censure [of grammar], because, like the case of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), the tradition of grammar is beginningless. Thus, the authority of grammar is directly presented by the Veda itself;
likewise, the *Arthavādins* declare: "Two sciences are to be known," so say those who know Brahman, "the higher and the lower.

Therein, the lower consists of the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, Atharvaveda, phonetics (*śikṣā*), ritual procedure (*kalpa*), grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), etymology (*nirukta*), prosody (*chandas*), and astronomy (*jyotiṣa*)."

Therefore, it is said: "This speech is uttered as that which has been explained.
And the explainers—Pāṇini, Kātyāyana, and Patañjali—are equal in authority to Manu and others.
Consequently, the Smṛti of Grammar is authoritative regarding the correct usage of words and the correctness of terms such as *go* (cow) and the like.

Regarding the injunction "one should sacrifice a horse" (*aśvam ālabheta*), if the letter situated between the vowel *a* and the semivowel *v* were dental, the meaning would become: "one should sacrifice one's own wealth (*svam* = *s-v-am*)—that is, one who is destitute, being devoid of that [wealth]."

Those two which are the word and its referent in common worldly usage do not exist in the Veda, or else they are different here;

Because the phonemes are identical, the word is identical; any difference in form is merely occasional.

The Vedic word and its meaning are different from the worldly word and its meaning.
Why? Because of the difference in form.

In common usage, the word *ātman* is fixed with the vowel *ā* at its beginning;

Therefore, having reached the position that "the words and word-meanings in the world and in the Veda are different," we reply: those very word-meanings which are worldly are the same as those which are Vedic.
For instance—the eternity of phonemes (*varṇa*) has already been established in the first chapter (*pāda*).

Just as, despite the difference among the persons who employ them, and despite the difference in the multiple utterances of each individual person, there is oneness of phoneme because of the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) that "these are those very same phonemes";

The identity of the words must be accepted on the basis of uncontradicted recognition, such as "those very same [words] being studied in the Veda.
However, the occasional difference in words, such as *ātmanā* versus *devāsaḥ*, is merely incidental;
one cannot set aside the unity of the word established by the more frequent instances of recognition on account of such exceptions.

Otherwise, even the identity of Devadatta as recognized in the cognition "This is that Devadatta" would be sublated by the mere difference of place and other factors. Furthermore, the unity of meaning necessarily follows from the unity of the word;
otherwise, since there would be no separate derivation [of meaning] for the Veda, the consequence would follow that it is non-expressive.
With this very point in mind, it has been said:
"A word whose capacity is understood from worldly usage is also expressive in the Veda.

Even though words such as *svaru*, *yūpa*, and *āhavanīya*, as well as their referents, are not known in the world, their primary signification (*vyutpatti*) is possible through co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with well-known words.
The description of being carried face-up and so forth, however, is merely an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda).
Or, even if such carrying were to occur, the words "face-up" and so on, as well as their respective meanings, are nonetheless established solely by worldly convention.
Therefore, those very words and word-meanings which are worldly are themselves the Vedic ones.
Starting with *Mīmāṃsājaiminīya-sūtra* 1.3.33–34,
he formulates the second section:
"Is the individual (*vyakti*) the meaning of words such as 'rice' (*vrīhi*), or is it the form (*ākṛti*), because of its connection with action?"
At the time of learning [the word], the individual instance (vyakti) is indicated by means of the form (ākṛti).
Based on arguments such as the apprehension of the word’s expressive power (*śakti*), it is appropriate that the form (*ākṛti*) is the meaning;
however, for the sake of the completion of the action, the individual instance (*vyakti*) should be understood there as the secondary indicator (*upalakṣya*).

In usages such as "one threshes rice" (*vrīhīnavahanti*), "one should sacrifice an animal" (*paśumālabheta*), "bring the cow" (*gāmānaya*), and "a Brahmin is not to be killed" (*brāhmaṇo na hantavyaḥ*), the meaning of words like "rice" (*vrīhi*) and so forth is the individual instance.
Why?
Because the individual instance (*vyakti*) can be connected with actions such as threshing;
for the generic form (*ākṛti*) is not capable of being threshed, sacrificed, or brought.
But surely, due to infinity and deviation, it is not possible for there to be linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*) with respect to individuals;
for individuals are infinite,
since it is impossible to determine the exact number of cows existing in various places throughout the past and the future.

Furthermore, if the word "cow" (go-śabda), having been learned in reference to a white individual, were then applied to a black individual, it would deviate from its own meaning. If it is asked, "How then was it learned [in that sense]?"—then, in that case, at the time of learning, that individual must have been characterized by its generic form (ākṛti). This being the conclusion:

We reply: Since it is through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the universal (*ākṛti*) is established as the cause for grasping the word's power (*śakti*), it is appropriate that the universal alone is the denotatum of the word.
Furthermore, when the word "cow" is uttered, one who maintains that the individual (*vyakti*) is the denotatum would experience doubt;
therefore, the universal alone is the object of expression.

If the actions such as threshing were not to culminate in the generic form (ākṛti), then the individual (vyakti) would have to be indicated there. Furthermore, in passages such as “one should pile the Śyena fire-altar,” it is observed that the generic form itself is connected to the ritual action by virtue of being the correlate of similarity.
Therefore, the generic form is the meaning of the word.
In this very context, he states the opinion of the Guru (Prabhākara):
"The injunction regarding cows and so forth cannot be our [source of knowledge], because there is no determination between the universal and the individual."
The conclusion is that the individual (vyakti) is not [the denotation], due to infinity and deviation.
The meaning is clear.

[Now begins the fourth quarter] (The first section, concerning the authority of words such as *udbhid* as names of sacrifices, contains the following sūtra).
"It has been stated that the Veda is for this purpose; therefore, everything [in it] must be for that purpose. (Jaimini Sūtra 1.4.1). This concludes the first section of the fourth quarter.

The author of the Vārttika sets forth the argument as follows: Is a word such as "udbhid" a means of valid knowledge regarding dharma, or is it not? It is not a means of valid knowledge because it is not included within the portions consisting of injunctions (vidhi), explanatory passages (arthavāda), or mantras.
The inclusion [of the word] within the injunction is seen in the case of "one should sacrifice with the *udbhid*";
its connection as a name within the sentence will be explained hereafter; therefore, that is indeed authoritative.
The texts are recited thus: "One should sacrifice with the *udbhid*," "One should sacrifice with the *balabhid*," and "One should sacrifice with the *viśvajit*."
In that regard, words such as "udbhid" are not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to *dharma*.
Why?
Because they are not included within the three divisions of the Veda which are accepted as being authoritative.
For instance: an injunction (*vidhi*) is a direct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
however, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and mantras function through their connection with an injunction.
In that regard, a word such as *udbhid* does not, first of all, fall within the scope of an injunction.

Because it does not express any of the constituent parts of the productive operation (bhāvanā)— which consists of the end to be accomplished (bhāvya), the instrument (karaṇa), and the procedure (itikartavyatā)—
nor is it an explanatory passage (arthavāda),
since there is no cognition of praise.
Nor is it a mantra,
because of the absence of mantra-indicative marks such as the "first person" (uttamapuruṣa) and so forth.
And thus it has been said:
"Because they lack the first person, the suffix -si, and forms such as the internal [suffixes],
and because of the absence of the established status of being a mantra, it is not logical for these to be considered mantras.
Thus, in the phrase "I offer what is pleasing to Agni," there is the first person.
“O Agni, glorious one, bestow glory upon me”—this is the invocation.
“Thou art wide and thou art wealthy”—this is its inner form.
“For food thee, for strength thee”—this is the *tvā*-form.

If it is argued that [the Veda] is not a means of valid cognition because the word "etc. includes the presentation of deities invoked by benediction (*āśīrdevatā*) and so forth, which are thus not included within these [categories], we say no;
for they are included within the instrument (*karaṇa*) as part of the injunctive element (*vidhyaṃśa*).

Although the meaning of the verbal root *yaj* (to sacrifice), which is presented within the same word, is the instrument by virtue of the optative suffix (*liṅ*), nevertheless, the word *udbhid* and so forth is construed with that *yaj* as its name.
Therefore, it is a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Or rather, it should be a name, because that which is new at its origin is not injunctive. (Jaimini Sūtra 1.4.3) [This is the sūtra in the second section concerning the fact that words such as *udbhid* are names of sacrifices. Jaim_1,4.2.
