"Based on its etymology, is this [word] a quality (*guṇa*) or a name (*nāmadheya*) for the spade?
Relying upon the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is an injunction of a quality for the sake of the animal sacrifice. (MJaiNy 1.4.3)
This etymological derivation [of the word "sacrifice"] from the manifestation of the fruit is the same even for that which is called a "sacrifice" (yāga);
its status as a name is appropriate because of its grammatical coreferentiality with the term "sacrifice."

In the injunction, "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *udbhid*," the meaning intended by the word *udbhid*, which ends in the instrumental case, would be some accessory (*guṇa*) in the sacrifice, because it is similar to the injunction of an accessory such as, "He offers oblation with curd.
Now, it might be argued: "The meaning of the word *dadhi* (curd) is well-known in common worldly usage."
"But the meaning of the word *udbhid* is not well-known"—
this is not so; for even in the absence of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), its meaning is established through the etymological analysis of its constituent parts.
Based on the etymology "that by which the earth is split," this word denotes a spade;
nor should it be said that some sacrifice having cattle as its fruit is enjoined here,
because cattle constitute a subordinate fruit [of an action].
Just as in the case of "for one desiring cattle, [one should use] a cow-milking vessel," where cattle are the fruit of the quality of the cow-milking vessel,
so too here let there be the fruit of the quality of the spade.
If the cow-milking vessel is enjoined by depending upon the previously established fetching of water prescribed in the rule, "one should fetch water with a *camasa*," [then it is a quality].
In that case, here too, let the spade be enjoined by depending on the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice which is established and under discussion in the injunction "One should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma.

Therefore, since it follows that this is an injunction of an accessory (guṇavidhi), we reply: the meaning of these two words, "one desiring cattle should sacrifice" (paśukāmo yajeta), is as follows: "One should bring about the fruit, namely cattle, by means of the sacrifice."
In that context, when there is the expectation "by what sacrifice?", the word ending in the instrumental case, *udbhidā*, connects as the name of the sacrifice.
Its status as a name is established through the etymological derivation (*nirukti*): "the fruit of cattle is split open (*udbhidyate*) by this sacrifice.

If it is argued that even so, there can be no definitive conclusion between the injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) and the status of being a name, because the verbal derivation is identical in both cases; [we reply:]...
Not so;
for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is the decisive factor.
When it is stated, "One should effect the fruit by means of a sacrifice characterized by [the root] *ud-bhid*," coreferentiality is thereby obtained.

If, however, [the instrumentality] were a quality (guṇatva), there would be a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), as in: "The sacrifice which is to be accomplished by means of a spade, by that [sacrifice].
If one were to apply coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) as "by a sacrifice possessing a spade," then the figurative indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) would result.
Therefore, words such as *udbhid* are names (*nāmadheya*).

In cases such as "one offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*) and "one should sacrifice with rice-grains" (*vrīhibhir yajeta*), because words like "curd" are extremely well-established (*atyanta-rūḍha*) in denoting specific substances, it is impossible for them to be names of sacrifices; thus, out of necessity, they are accepted as denoting qualities (*guṇa*).

In the case of "one should sacrifice with soma" (*somena yajeta*) as well, rather than postulating a name whose meaning is not well-established, it is better [to accept it] by way of its well-established meaning.
Intending to resort to *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication), the indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*)—namely, "by means of a sacrifice possessing the substance Soma"—is accepted.
However, since the word *udbhid* lacks a meaning established by common worldly usage, its status as a name (*nāmadheya*) is appropriate according to the aforementioned method.
As for the purpose of a name, it is simply for the sake of conventional designation in all cases.
For indeed, apart from a name, there is no easy means of identifying [the deity] in acts such as the selection of officiating priests, [expressed as] "I shall sacrifice with this.
Therefore,
*udbhid* and so forth are names.
START MJaiNy 1.4.5.
On this very point, he states the opinion of the Guru: "If it is argued that this injunction is dependent [on other factors] in the case of a worldly *gaṇayāga*,"
Because the name of the Vedic sacrifice is established through etymological derivation (*nirukti*), it possesses independence.
[Commentary: In the injunction "one should sacrifice with the *udbhid*," this is an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*).
However, no Vedic basis (*āśraya*) for it is found.
Therefore, worldly practices such as the sacrifice to the group of Mothers (mātṛgaṇayāga) would have to be depended upon as its basis;
however, that is not the case in this yoga.
For, according to the previously stated etymological derivation, since it is the name of a Vedic sacrifice, it is independent [of external factors].
Jaimini Sūtra 1.4.6–7 (In the third section, concerning the topic that words such as *citrā* are names of sacrifices):
"That in which there is an instruction regarding a quality, [that word is a name], because it is connected primarily with the principal act. (Jaimini 1.4.3)

The third section formulates the problem: "In the injunction 'one should sacrifice with the Citrā,' it must be either a quality or a name; because of conventional usage, it refers to the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma as possessing the quality of being variegated and female."
If both were enjoined, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*); if there were a relation of qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*), there would be prolixity (*gaurava*).
This may indeed be the case for the *pṛṣṭha*, *ājya*, and *bahiṣpavamāna* [stotras], as it is so in those instances.
The text "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *citrā*" is thus handed down in the scripture.
In this context, the word *citrā* is not etymological (*yaugika*) like the word *udbhid*; rather, by virtue of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), it denotes both variegatedness and femininity.
Therefore, its status as a name (*nāmadheya*) does not follow the previous logical principle.

This being the case, the following might be argued: having referred to the animal sacrifice alone—which was enjoined by the injunction "One should immolate an animal for Agni and Soma"—by means of the word "yajeta" ("one should sacrifice"), the two qualities of variegated color and femininity are then enjoined with respect to that animal.
To this we reply: these two qualities, namely variegated color and femininity, [are both enjoined].
If both of these were enjoined, the sentence would suffer from syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
As it has been said:
"When the ritual act is already established, more than one accessory (*guṇa*) cannot be enjoined."
"But when [multiple things] are not yet established, even many are enjoined with a single effort.

Alternatively, if—in order to avoid the fault of syntactical split (vākyabheda)—the factor (kāraka) consisting of the sacrificial substance (dravya), namely the animal, qualified by two attributes were to be enjoined, then there would be excessive complexity (gaurava).
Therefore, as before, the word *citrā* is the name of a sacrifice (*yajñanāmadheya*) through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the root *yaji*.
Its variegated nature, however, is established by way of distinct substances,
such as curd, honey, and ghee.
Water, parched grains, and rice grains.
"That which is mixed with that is the *prājāpatya* [offering]"—thus, six various substances to be offered, such as curd and the like, are prescribed.
This is the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) for the sacrifice named *Citrā*, because here both the substance (curd, etc.
and the deity (Prajāpati), which constitute the essential form of the sacrifice, are taught.
Once that sacrifice has arisen, the sentence "one desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā" serves as its fruit-statement (*phalavākya*).
This being the case, the subject matter under discussion (*prakṛta*) is maintained.

If, however, a quality were enjoined by way of a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, there would result the abandonment of the subject matter at hand (*prakṛtahāna*) and the introduction of a subject matter not under discussion (*aprakṛtaprakriyā*).
Since it must be admitted that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) functions as a restatement (*anuvādaka*), the primary injunctive meaning would be sublated.
Therefore, the word *citrā* is a name (*nāmadheya*). Just as the word *citrā* [in the previous example] is a name.
In the same way, the status of being a name [of a rite] should be applied to the term *bahiṣpavamāna*, as well as to the terms *ājya* and *pṛṣṭha*.
For it is heard thus: "The *bahispavamāna* is threefold," "The *ājya* hymns are fifteenfold," and "The *pṛṣṭha* hymns are seventeenfold.
The meaning of these three statements is explained as follows:
in the *uttaragrantha* of the Sāmavedins, hymns (*sūkta*) consisting of triplets (*ṛca*) are recorded.
In that regard, “*Upāsmai gāyatā naraḥ*,” etc., is the first *sūkta*;
“*Davidyutatyā rucā*,” etc., is the second; and “*Pāvamānasya te kave*,” etc., is the third.

In the performance of the morning libation (*prātaḥsavana*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the Gāyatra Sāman is to be chanted upon those three hymns (*sūkta*). This stotra, accomplished by chanting over the triad of hymns, is called the *bahiṣpavamāna*, because the verses situated therein are for the purpose of the Pavamāna [deity] and because of their connection with the exterior.
Indeed, this hymn is not employed within the pavilion named *sadas* in the vicinity of the *audumbarī* pillar, as other hymns are;
rather, it is employed by those moving outside the *sadas*. And for that *bahiṣpavamāna*, there is a *stoma* named *trivṛt*.

And the Brāhmaṇa passage prescribing that *stoma* is handed down as follows: “He utters *hiṃ* for three [verses] with the first; he utters *hiṃ* for three [verses] with the middle one; he utters *hiṃ* for three [verses] with the last; this is the *viṣṭuti* of the *trivṛt*.”
The meaning is this: the singing of the nine verses contained in the three hymns must be performed in three rounds (*paryāya*).
Among them, in the first round, the first four verses of each of the three hymns are to be sung;
in the second round, the middle [verses].
And in the third instance, they are the best.
The ablative case in "tisṛbhyaḥ" is used in the sense of the instrumental;
the meaning is that he utters the sound *hiṃ* and sings.
This song, endowed with the aforementioned manner, is the *viṣṭuti*—a specific mode of praise—of the *trivṛt-stoma*. This *viṣṭuti* is named "The Rising" (*udyatī*).
Thus, there are two *viṣṭutis*: "The Turning Back" (*parivartinī*) and "The Nest-like" (*kulāyinī*).

Regarding these two [turns], it is handed down in the tradition as follows: “He makes the sound *hiṃ* after three [verses] with [them] in direct order; he makes the sound *hiṃ* after three [verses] with [them] in direct order; he makes the sound *hiṃ* after three [verses] with [them] in direct order.”
"The *trivṛt* *viṣṭuti* is the *parivartinī*. This means [it is performed] with verses recited in their natural sequence (*parācībhiḥ*).
The *kulāyinī* is thus recited: "He utters *hiṃ* after three [verses]; he utters *hiṃ* after three [verses] in their natural sequence (*parācībhiḥ*)."
That which is middling is the first;
that which is inferior is the middling; that which is first is the best.
He utters "hiṃ" three times: that which is the last becomes the first,
that which was the first becomes the middle, and that which was the middle becomes the last.
"The *kulāyinī* is the threefold *viṣṭuti*.
In this regard, in the first hymn, the order is simply that of recitation;
in the second, it is the middle, the last, and the first.

In the third [stoma], however, the mantras are to be chanted by way of transposition as "the best, the first, and the middle. These three modes of chanting (viṣṭuti) are thus presented as alternatives.
Such is the meaning of the term *trivṛt* as the nature of this stoma.
However, it was determined in the previous section (*pūrvapāda*) that [the *sāman*] does not consist of the three qualities (*traiguṇya*).
In the subsequent text, four hymns (*sūkta*) are recited after the three *bahiṣpavamāna* hymns: the first hymn begins with "O Agni, come for the feast" (*agna ā yāhi vītaye*);
the second is "Come to us, O Mitra and Varuṇa" (*ā no mitrāvaruṇa*).
“*Ā yāhi suṣumā hi te*” is the third;
“*Indrāgnī ā gataṃ sutam*” is the fourth.
These four Ājya-stotras, being sung at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) with the Gāyatra-sāman, are so called.

And their etymological explanation is heard: "Because they went toward the race (*ājim*), that is the reason for the *ājya* nature of the *ājyas*. In those *ājya-stotras*, there is a chant-form (*stoma*) named Pañcadaśa (the fifteenfold).

The *viṣṭuti* (method of chanting) for that *stoma* is handed down as follows: “He utters *hiṃ* five times: three [verses] with one [repetition], one with one, and one with one; he utters *hiṃ* five times: one with one, three with one, and one with one; he utters *hiṃ* five times: one with one, one with one, and three with one.
Thus, a single hymn (*sūkta*) is to be repeated three times.
In that regard, in the first recitation there is a triple repetition of the first verse;
in the second recitation, of the middle verse;
and in the third recitation, of the last verse.
This is the fifteen-fold hymn-form (*pañcadaśastoma*).

Following the four hymns already mentioned, three Mādhyandina-pavamāna hymns are recited in the *Uttara-grantha*, and after those, four further hymns are recited; among these, the first begins with “*Abhi tvā śūra nonuma*.”
“By what means will the wondrous one come to us? is the second [verse].
“Him, your wonder-worker, the subduer of enemies,” is the third.
“With your aids, [we call] the finder of wealth,” is the fourth.
These, being chanted at the midday pressing with the *rathantara*, *vāmadevya*, *naudhasa*, and *kāleya* *sāmans* respectively, are called the *pṛṣṭha-stotras*.
The etymological derivation should be understood as: "They are *pṛṣṭhas* because of their touching (*sparśanāt*). In these stotras, the seventeenfold hymn-form (*saptadaśa-stoma*) is employed.
The *viṣṭuti* (recitation method) of that *stoma* is handed down in the tradition as follows: “He utters *hiṃ* for five [verses]: three times with three [verses], once with one, and once with one;
he utters *hiṃ* for five [verses]: once with one, three times with three, and once with one; he utters *hiṃ* for five [verses]: once with one, three times with three, and once with one.”
"For he performs [the recitation] for seven [verses]: once with one [verse], three times with three [verses], and three times with three [verses].
Here, in the first round, there is a triple repetition of the first verse;
in the second round, of the middle verse.
In the third recitation, during the middle and highest [stomas], this is the seventeen-fold stoma (*saptadaśastoma*).
Here, in all three sentences, the words *trivṛt*, *pañcadaśa*, and *saptadaśa* are accepted as enjoining qualities (*guṇavidhi*).
If the words *bahiṣpavamāna*, *ājya*, and *pṛṣṭha* were also enjoiners of qualities, then each would constitute a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*).
Alternatively, because two distinct qualities would have to be enjoined, there would be a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*).
Therefore, words such as *bahiṣpavamāna* are names of the stotras.
Having referred to the rites by means of these names, the qualities such as the *trivṛt* are enjoined.
And there is another scriptural passage that makes that [name] known.

Jaimini Sūtra 1.4.4. (In the fourth section, concerning the status of words such as *agnihotra* as names of sacrifices, the *matprakhyanyāya* [the principle of "that which makes it known"], the aphorism:
And there is another scriptural passage that makes that [name] known. Jaimini Sūtra 1.4.4.

The fourth section formulates the problem: "He offers the Agnihotra; he pours the Āghāra"—are these two [acts] injunctions for a quality and a preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*), or rather are they names of rituals?

In the expression "agnaye hotram asya," the word *anala* (fire) contained within the *bahuvrīhi* compound would be the quality to be enjoined if it were a name; otherwise, the form [of the word] would not apply to the flowing ghee.

It has been stated that "one pours the Āghāra" refers to a preparatory act (saṃskriyā), as indicated by the accusative case; furthermore, "Āghāra" and "Agnihotra" are both etymological names for the ritual action itself.

From the mantra "Agni is light," the deity is thus obtained, as is the clarified butter (ghṛta) mentioned in the statement regarding the fourfold taking; however, this is the interpretation for the accusative case.
For when the meaning of the verbal root has not yet been accomplished, that [root] possesses the status of an instrument;
therefore, its state of being an object (sādhya) is expressed by the refinement (*saṃskāra*). Because it is an action (*kriyā*), it cannot even be suspected [to be anything else].

In the cases of "He offers the *agnihotra*" (*agnihotraṃ juhoti*) and "He pours the *āghāra* libation" (*āghāram āghārayati*), if the word *agnihotra* were merely a name for a ritual (*karmanāman*), then due to the absence of both substance (*dravya*) and deity (*devatā*), the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the sacrifice would not be established.
Therefore, by this [text], the quality consisting of the deity Agni is enjoined for the *darvihoma* offering.
Furthermore, the word *āghāra* is derived from the verbal root *ghṛ*, meaning "to flow" or "to shine," and thus it denotes flowing clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
And in that clarified butter, its status as the object to be refined (*saṃskārya*) is understood through the accusative case-ending.
And that prepared ghee becomes the substance for the *upāṃśuyāja* sacrifice;
therefore, since it has been argued that "the words *agnihotra* and *āghāra* are injunctions of accessory qualities (*guṇa*) and preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*),"—

We reply: Since the deities are already established by the mantras prescribed in the injunctions, "One offers in the evening with the mantra, 'Agni is light, light is Agni, svāhā! and "In the morning with the mantra, 'Sūrya is light, light is Sūrya, svāhā!'," the deities are not themselves objects of injunction.
Therefore, the term *agnihotra* is an etymological name for that ritual which must be performed regularly in the evening and morning, having Agni and Sūrya as its deities.

And the etymological derivation (*yoga*) is shown by means of a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Since the substance of clarified butter (*ājya*) is already established by the very statement, "This [butter] was taken four times; having poured the *āghāra* for it," the act of consecrating the flowing ghee cannot be the object of an injunction; therefore, the word *āghāra* is also an etymological name for the ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*).

"The name of that rite in which clarified butter is poured continuously, beginning from the southwestern direction (nairṛtī) and making the northeastern direction (aiśānī) its limit, is this [‘āghāra’]. But surely, if it is a name, then— as in cases such as ‘one should sacrifice with the udbhid’ or ‘one should sacrifice with the jyotiṣṭoma’— there ought to be an instrumental case ending for the sake of grammatical coordination with the instrument that is the meaning of the verbal root, as in ‘one offers oblations with the agnihotra’ or ‘one pours the āghāra with the āghāra’."

This is not a fault. Since the object (*artha*) has already attained the state of being accomplished (*siddha*) after the performance of the rite, even though it functions as an instrument (*karaṇa*), it is appropriate to use the accusative case—such as *agnihotram* or *āghāram*—to express its state of being something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) prior to that.
Furthermore, one should not suspect, on the basis of this accusative usage, that there is a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) here as in the case of "he sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*).
Just like the word *vrīhi* (rice), since the words *agnihotra* and *āghāra* lack the status of denoting well-known substances (*prasiddhadravya*), they must be accepted as denoting actions.

Therefore, the words *agnihotra* and *āghāra* do not enjoin accessories (*guṇa*) or preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*) for the *darvihoma* and *upāṃśuyāja* respectively; rather, they are the names of two distinct rituals.

Just as in the expression "like a hawk" (śyena), there is a relationship between a standard of comparison and the object compared;
since these two cannot exist in a single entity, this [term] must function as the name of a ritual action (karmanāman).

In the case of the injunction "One desiring to practice sorcery should sacrifice with the Śyena," if it were the name of a ritual action, the very nature of the sacrifice would not be established, because of the absence of both a material substance (dravya) and a deity (devatā).

Consequently, in the Soma sacrifice, the constant substance *soma* being set aside, a desirable accessory (*guṇa*) in the form of the substance "bird" is enjoined in place of *soma*. Therefore, since the quality of the bird— the standard of comparison— exists in the ritual action which is the object of comparison, the word *śyena* (hawk) is the name of the *abhicāra* rite. In the passages, "One should sacrifice with the *saṃdaṃśa*" and "One being afflicted by cattle should sacrifice," the status of the words *saṃdaṃśa* and *go* as names should be understood in the same way as that of the word *śyena*.

This is because the relationship between the object of comparison and the thing compared is expressed by the two supplementary phrases: "just as one takes up that which is difficult to grasp with a pair of tongs" and "just as cows protect [their calves]."

And that [yajati] is common to both the state of being an object (*karmatva*) and the state of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*). Indeed, no specific case-ending is heard there that directly denotes either the state of being an object or the state of being an instrument.

Because it is included within [the primary rite], there would be a name [for it] starting with "eightfold" (aṣṭatādi), just as in the case of the Agnihotra;
if it were not a substance [included] within another substance, then it would be a quality (guṇa) with respect to the fruit.
The unity of the sentence is clear from the concluding summary, yet that is set aside when there is an injunction of multiple qualities; therefore, through the parts, there is praise of the whole.

In the section on optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭi*), it is heard: "When a son is born, one should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara. "In that there is a cake on eight potsherds, by means of the *gāyatrī* verse he purifies him with Vedic splendor (*brahmavarcasa*); in that there is a cake on nine potsherds, by means of the *trivṛt* [stoma] he bestows brilliance upon him; in that there is a cake on ten potsherds, by means of the *virāj* [metre] he bestows food upon him."
"In that it has eleven potsherds, he bestows sensory power upon him by means of the Triṣṭubh; in that it has twelve potsherds, he bestows cattle upon him by means of the Jagatī.
He for whom, once born, one performs this sacrifice, becomes purified, radiant, an eater of food, endowed with sensory power, and possessed of cattle."

In this context, because of the commonality of numbers such as eight and so forth, the nature of the *gāyatrī* and other meters is metaphorically attributed to the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) and the like.

Since the number twelve mentioned in the injunction for the sacrifice includes within itself numbers such as eight and so on, one view is that, based upon those numbers, terms such as "eight-pot-sherd" (*aṣṭākapāla*) are names of the ritual acts, just like the term "agnihotra. This is the first position.
In this context, the term *dvādaśakapāla* does not refer to a number, but rather to the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) as its substance;
for its etymological derivation is "that which is prepared upon twelve potsherds."
The same applies to words such as *aṣṭākapāla* and so forth.
If it is argued that this being the case, since one substance is not included within another substance, there is no basis for a name [to apply],
then let a quality characterized by the form of the *puroḍāśa* be enjoined.
Nor should it be argued that there is no room for the eight-potsherd [offering] because it is already occupied by the cake on twelve potsherds prescribed for the originative injunction;
for another view holds that the injunction of that [eight-potsherd offering] is justified for the sake of results such as spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). This view, too, is tenable.
Because if one were to enjoin many qualities [simultaneously], it would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
Nor should it be argued that these are indeed distinct sentences;

for, from the concluding statement—"on whose birth he offers this"—it is understood that there is a single syntactical unity with the injunction "one should offer the Vaiśvānara cake on twelve potsherds."
Therefore, the twelve-potsherd offering, as the whole, is praised by means of its parts, such as the eight-potsherd offering and others.
START MJaiNy 1.4.36.
Here, he states the opinion of the Guru:
"Because it lacks qualities, because it is not a name, because it is not a mantra, and because there is no connection..."
If it is argued that [the passage] is not a means of valid knowledge because it consists of eight [syllables], etc., we say no, because it is connected as an explanatory statement (arthavāda).
According to the reasoning already stated, its being a subordinate element (guṇatva) or a name (nāmatva) is impossible;
furthermore, it is not a mantra because it lacks the second-person address and other characteristics of a mantra.
If it is argued that, because the eight-pot-sherd offerings (*aṣṭākapāla*) and so forth cannot be syntactically connected [to the injunction], the sentence lacks authority (*aprāmāṇya*), we say:
not so;
for it has been stated that they are connected by way of being commendatory (*stāvaka*).

The accomplishment of that [is established]. Jaimini Sūtra 1.4.23. (In the thirteenth section, concerning the fact that the word "sacrificer" serves as a praise for the sacrificial grass-bundle and so forth, there is this aphorism: "The accomplishment of that. Jaimini Sūtra 1.4.37–39.
He formulates the thirteenth section:
"In this case, is the sacrificer the *prastara* (grass-bundle), or is it a quality (*guṇa*), or a name (*nāman*), or a praise (*stuti*)?
Through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), one would be the name of the other."
Or rather, let the sacrificer be the quality [predicated] of the sacrificial grass-bundle (prastara) indicated by its function;
however, as in the previous case, there is no figurative praise here due to the absence of a relationship between part and whole.

If it were argued that because of the difference in meaning the word lacks the status of a name and thus expresses a quality (*guṇa*), then that [quality] would be praised by way of its being an instrument for accomplishing the sacrifice; this is a praise of the *prastara* (grass-bundle) as something to be enjoined.
This is recorded in the scripture: “The sacrificer is the *prastara*.”
In this regard, one view is that the word *prastara* is a name for the sacrificer, or the word *yajamāna* is a name for the *prastara*;
why? Because of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), as in the case of "by means of the *udbhid* vehicle," and so forth. This is one position.
Another view is that this is an injunction of a subordinate quality (guṇavidhi).

Even in that case, since the unconscious sacrificial grass-bundle (prastara) lacks the capacity for the duties of the sacrificer such as recitation (japa) and so forth, it cannot possess the status of a subordinate quality.

However, because the sacrificer is capable of performing the duties of the grass-bundle such as holding the offering-ladle (sruk), the subordinate quality consisting of the sacrificer himself is enjoined.

This being the case, although the word *prastara*, heard later, indicates the function [of the sacrificer], the word *yajamāna*, heard first, retains its primary (literal) sense. Furthermore, praise cannot be established here by the previous principle,
because there is no relationship of part and whole between the *prastara* and the sacrificer, as there is between the eight-pot-sherd cake and the twelve-pot-sherd cake.
If it is argued that this is a mere praise (stuti), as in the passage, "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity, for the attainment of vigor," and so forth—no;
for, unlike [the mention of] attributes such as swiftness, no excellence of any kind is perceived here.
Therefore, since the conclusion reached is that [the mantra] must be either a name (nāman) or a statement of qualities (guṇa)—
We reply: Since the difference in meaning between "cow" (*go*) and "buffalo" (*mahiṣa*) is extremely well known, it is not proper for [the word *yajamāna*] to be a name (*nāmadheya*).

However, in the case of it being a quality (*guṇa*), since the throwing into the fire is the function of the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*), if the sacrificer were thrown in, there would be a failure of the ritual (*karmalopa*).
Therefore, the sacrificial grass-bundle, which is the object of the injunction, is praised by means of the word "sacrificer."

Just as in the expression "Devadatta is a lion," Devadatta— who is endowed with qualities such as bravery characteristic of a lion— is praised by means of the word "lion," so too the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*), which is possessed of the quality of being an instrument for the sacrifice belonging to the sacrificer, is praised by means of the word "sacrificer. This same principle is to be understood in cases such as "The sacrificer is the one-pot-sherd [cake]," and so forth.

Jātiḥ. (Sūtra in the section concerning the fact that the fourteen words beginning with "āgneya" serve as praises for the Brāhmaṇas and others; Jaimini Sūtra 1.4.40). Jāti [is the meaning]. Jaimini 1.4.24.
He formulates the fourteenth section:
"In this case as well, the Brāhmaṇa belongs to Agni; the entire determination is as before.
However, the door [to the discussion] lies in the praise [of the Brāhmaṇa] by virtue of his being born from the mouth and belonging to Agni."
This is handed down in tradition: “The Brāhmaṇa is indeed *āgneya*.

Here, because there is an absolute difference in the well-known meanings [of the two words], the word *āgneya* is not the name of the Brāhmaṇa, nor is a quality consisting in having Agni as its deity enjoined.
"An *āgneya* hymn," "an *āgneya* oblation"— since a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) expressing a deity has as its scope only hymns and oblations;
for a Brahmin is neither a hymn nor an oblation.
Therefore, the Brāhmaṇa is praised by means of the word *Āgneya*, which ends in a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) expressing a relationship;
for although there is no direct connection with fire in the Brāhmaṇa,
nevertheless, the quality of being born from the mouth— which is connected to fire— is present in the Brāhmaṇa.

Likewise, the fact that both fire and the Brāhmaṇa were produced from the mouth is recorded in a certain explanatory passage (arthavāda): “Prajāpati desired, ‘May I create offspring. He fashioned the Trivṛt [stoma] from his mouth.”
Agni was yoked as the deity,
the Gāyatrī as the metre, and the Rathantara as the Sāman.
“The Brāhmaṇa is the foremost among humans,
and the goat among animals; therefore they are preeminent, for they were created from the mouth.”
Therefore, the word "Āgneya" is laudatory.
The same should be understood in cases such as "The Rājanya is Aindra" and "The Vaiśya is Vaiśvadeva," and so forth. (Mīmāṃsā Nyāya Candrikā 1.4.40)
Jaimini Sūtra 1.4.41 (The section concerning the fact that words such as "sacrificial post" [yūpa] in the fifteenth [section] serve to praise the sacrificer):
Because of similarity of form. Jaimini 1.4.25.
The fifteenth section formulates the following:
In the statement "The sacrificial post is the sun," there is praise by means of the word "sun";
and the door [to that praise] is the similarity with the visual organ, which exists in the ghee-smeared, metallic [post]. (MJaiNy 1.4.41)
The brilliance that is perceivable by the eye in the sun is also present in the sacrificial post (*yūpa*),
because of the determination of the sacrificial post smeared with clarified butter as being brilliant.
Therefore, the sacrificial post is praised by means of the word "sun."

Thus, in the passage "The sacrificer is the sacrificial post" (yajamāno yūpaḥ), the sacrificial post is praised by means of the word "sacrificer" because of the commonality of the upwardness perceptible to the eye.

Praise. Jaimini Sūtra 1.4.42–44 (In the sixteenth section [of the first chapter], concerning the fact that words such as "non-cow" and others serve the purpose of praising cows and other things). Praise. Jaimini Sūtra 1.4.26.
The sixteenth section formulates the following:

"Other than cows and horses, animals are either non-animals or [are] animals"—thus it is heard in the Śruti. Regarding goats and the like, is that which is called "non-animal" a figurative statement (guṇavāda) based on some quality, or is it to be taken literally? MJaiNy_1,4.42 //
Because there is an absence of praise, the quality in those [words] is the prohibition of animal-sacrificial acts;
for a prohibition is impossible with words that denote objects such as jars and the like.
By the word "non-animals" (*apaśu*), animals are indicated through the commonality of the absence of excellence;
however, in that context, the basis for the indication is indeed the praise of cows and horses.
This is recorded in the tradition: "Other than cows and horses, all others are indeed non-animals."
"Animals are cows and horses. In that context, the non-animal status heard with respect to goats and the like cannot function as an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise),
because no praise is perceived through the mere negation of animal status.
If it is argued that, consequently, a quality consisting in the prohibition of animal sacrifice is being enjoined,
this is not so;
for it would be impossible to prohibit such acts, as that would entail the absurdity of rendering injunctions regarding animals such as goats and others purposeless.
The word *apaśu* denotes the entire class of objects such as jars and the like, which are distinct from cattle (*paśu*).
In those objects, such as jars, there is no excellence (*prāśastya*) comparable to that found in cows and horses.

Since this absence of excellence exists in animals such as goats, with this intention, goats and the like—though they are indeed cattle—are indicated by the term *apaśu* due to their similarity to jars and other such objects.

In the previous case, the grounds for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of words such as "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*) to objects such as the "grass-bundle" (*prastara*) were [figurative], and the result of that application was the praise of the grass-bundle and so forth. Here, however, in the application of the word "non-animal" (*apaśu*) to goats and the like, the very praise of cattle and horses is both the ground for its application and its result.
Praise is of two kinds: one kind is the excellence of qualities existing in the object itself;
the other kind is the excellence of qualities produced by the praising word.
The excellence of cows and horses over goats and the like, which is established in the world, serves as the basis for this [distinction].
"Although goats and others are by nature animals (*paśu*), they have become non-animals (*apaśu*) in relation to cows and horses;
such is the greatness of cows and horses"—this is the fruit of the praise.
Therefore, the statement "they are indeed non-animals" is an *arthavāda* (explanatory eulogy).
This same principle should be applied to other examples as well: "That which is without *sāman* is indeed not a sacrifice (*ayajña*)" is one example;
"That which is without *chandas* is indeed not a *sattra*" is another example.
Even a sacrifice such as the *Agnihotra*, *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, and so forth, becomes a non-sacrifice (*ayajña*) due to the absence of the *sāman*.
Such is the greatness of the Sāman;
by the term *chandoga*, the twenty-fourth and the forty-fourth [stomas] are indicated.
These three are called the *stomas* of forty-eight;

they are so named because they are sung with the *gāyatrī*, *triṣṭubh*, and *jagatī* meters due to the equality in the number of their syllables. Their specific arrangement (*viṣṭuti*) is to be found in the *Sāmaveda-Brāhmaṇa*.
Therefore, even a sacrificial session (*satra*) consisting of fourteen nights or more becomes a non-session (*asatra*) because it is devoid of *Chandogas*.
Such is the greatness of the *Chandogas*.
Thus, because it functions as a praise, it is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
The Abundance (bhūman). Jaimini Sūtra 1.4.45–48 (in the seventeenth section concerning the designation of creation by means of abundance, the aphorism). Jaimini Sūtra 1.4.27: The Abundance.
He formulates the seventeenth section as follows:

"Regarding the statement 'he lays down the sṛṣṭi-bricks,' those mantras characterized by the word 'sṛṣṭi' are either to be enjoined as subordinate elements (guṇa), or there is a descriptive praise (vāda) here; the injunction pertains to the subordinate element."
Because of the connection with a verb, because of the absence of connection with another injunction,
and because the mantras obtain their application through indicative power (liṅga) and context (prakaraṇa), an injunction [of the mantras] is impossible.
Having referred to those [verses], one should prescribe the laying of the bricks because they are to be praised;
therefore, the statement "the Sṛṣṭis" by means of the phrase "according to their creation" is an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda).
In certain mantra collections such as "ekayāstuvat," the word *sṛṣṭi* does not occur;
nevertheless, the expression [uses] the word *sṛṣṭi* because of its abundance [of meaning].
In the context of the fire-altar piling (*agnicayana*), it is heard in the scripture: "One piles the *sṛṣṭis*."
Those bricks for the laying down of which there exist mantras containing the word *sṛṣṭi* (creation) are called *sṛṣṭis*.

This is derived by analyzing the compound as "the laying-down mantra of these is characterized by *sṛṣṭi*" (*sṛṣṭir mānā āsām upadhāno mantraḥ*), according to the grammatical derivation established by Pāṇinian rules such as *tadvāmāsām upadhānaḥ* (Pā.
Sū. 4.4.125). Furthermore, the laying-down mantras containing the word *sṛṣṭi* are recited in this section (*anuvāka*) beginning with "They praised with one" (*ekayāstuvata*).
Because the verbal root *sṛj* (to create) is employed in reference to them in such passages as “Brahmā was created,
the elements were created,” those mantras are here enjoined as subordinate elements (*guṇa*) under the name of “creation” (*sṛṣṭi*) during the act of placing the bricks.
Why? Because of its connection with the verb "he places" (*upadadhāti*).

Furthermore, it is not possible for this [sentence] to be a mere explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), because it lacks syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) with any other injunction. This being the position reached—
We reply: Since those mantras are recited in the context of the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*), their general connection with the piling is understood.
Their specific connection, however, must be understood from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the word "creates" (*sṛjati*).
This being the case, since [the connection] is already established, those mantras are not enjoined here.
However, having recited those mantras, the laying down of the bricks is enjoined.
The recitation by means of the word "creation" (sṛṣṭi) is for the purpose of making possible the explanatory passage (arthavāda) that is about to be stated;
for the explanatory passage to be stated will be: "He obtains [the bricks] exactly as they were created."

If the word "creation" (*sṛṣṭi*) in the injunctive sentence were not a restatement of the mantras, then, because of the use of the word "creation" in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), there would arise the misconception of a lack of coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) between the injunction and the explanatory passage.
Therefore, the word "creation," which restates the mantras, does not enjoin a subordinate quality (*guṇa*).
But this is merely an explanatory statement (arthavāda).
Now, it may be argued that in the first mantra the root *sṛj* (to create) is not employed, but rather the root *dhā* (to place) is used.
This is because of the textual reading: “They praised with one [verse], ‘creatures were produced’.
Certainly;
nevertheless, since the verbal root *sṛj* (to create) is employed in many mantras from the second and third onwards, there exists a similarity in the form of smoke.
Where all sentences are accompanied by words denoting creation, there the application of the word "creation" is as it is [in the case of the model sacrifice].

Jaimini Sūtra 1.4.49 (in the eighteenth section concerning the principle of the collection of indicative marks, specifically the section [adhikaraṇa] on the fact that words such as "possessing breath" (*prāṇabhṛt*) serve the purpose of praise):
Because of the inherent connection with the indicative mark. Jaim_1,4.28.
He formulates the eighteenth topic:
"Like the creation [mantra], there is similarity with respect to the living beings therein, due to the abundance of indicative marks (*liṅga*);
here, the coexistence of indicative marks within a single mantra is distinguished. (MJaiNy 1.4.49)
Regarding the statement, “He lays down the *prāṇabhṛt* [bricks],” the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that this is an injunction of mantras according to the principle of creation (*sṛṣṭinyāya*).
However, it is actually an injunction for the laying down of bricks by way of a restatement (*anuvāda*) of mantras already established through indicative power (*liṅga*) and context (*prakaraṇa*).

The restatement of the mantras by the term *prāṇabhṛt* serves to justify the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) to be stated later: “Verily, he thereby bestows the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) upon this very [altar].”
In the preceding section—the mantras concerning the second layer and so forth—there is an abundance of signs of creation (*sṛṣṭi*).
Here, however, the sign of the breath-bearers (*prāṇabhṛt*) is recorded in the very first mantra: "This one who was in front, his breath is Bhauvāyana.

Even though only a single mantra possesses the status of a breath-bearer, all the mantras associated with it are indicated by the term "breath-bearer," just as in the expression, "The umbrella-bearers are going."
Thus, the grounds for figurative usage (*guṇavṛtti*), such as the accomplishment of the sacrificer’s purpose, have been determined.
And so it has been said:
"By means of [the accomplishment of] that, genus, similarity, praise, indicative mark, and abundance..."

"In six cases, a figurative application of words is established everywhere. (Thus ends the section on the determination of doubtful meanings by means of supplementary statements in the nineteenth [adhikaraṇa], sutra 1.4.50–53.)
"In cases of doubt, [the meaning is determined] from the remainder of the sentence" (Jaimini 1.4.29).
The nineteenth section formulates the following problem:
"He places pebbles smeared with ghee; for ghee is indeed brilliance. What is the purpose here?"
The collyrium is smeared with oil and the like, or else it is anointed with clarified butter.
Even by means of oil and the like, [the former] prevails because it is primary, because no contradiction has yet arisen,
because its object has not been previously established, and because this injunction is stronger due to its being a direct statement.
The general rule is not to be performed, for there is no specific injunction;
rather, the application must be with clarified butter (ghṛta) alone, because the doubt is resolved by the remainder of the sentence (vākyaśeṣa).

This praise, contained within an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), having approached the clarified butter (*ghṛta*), makes known the status of the clarified butter as something to be performed, and thereby leads to the understanding of the injunction (*vidhi*).
It is heard in scripture: "He places the pebbles smeared [with ghee]" and "Clarified butter is indeed brilliance."
Small stones mixed with clay are called *śarkarā*;
these should be smeared with any one of the substances such as clarified butter (*ghṛta*), oil (*taila*), or fat (*vasā*).
Why?

This is because an injunctive sentence that conveys a general substance such as "ointment" is more powerful than an explanatory passage (arthavāda) that conveys a specific substance such as "clarified butter.
And regarding its superiority, there are three reasons: primacy and so forth.
Primacy belongs to the injunction because it expresses its own primary meaning.
Furthermore, because it is heard first, there is no contradiction [with what precedes];

because it makes known an object not yet understood, it possesses an independent meaning; as for the explanatory passage (arthavāda), however, it is not primary because its purpose is to praise the injunction.
Because it is heard last, it is contradicted [by what precedes]; because it restates a matter already known, its meaning is already established.
Therefore, when the rule "ointment may be applied by anyone at all" would otherwise apply—
We reply: By an injunctive sentence, is the general means of application enjoined, or its specific variety?
Not the first.
The first [alternative] is not tenable because a universal cannot be put into practice;
nor is the second,
because there is no word that denotes specific instances such as ghee, oil, and so forth.

Therefore, according to the reasoning stated above, even a powerful injunctive statement requires an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) as a basis for determination by generating doubt regarding the specific details suitable for performance; it does not, however, contradict such a passage.
If it is argued that there is likewise no injunction regarding clarified butter (*ghṛta*) within the explanatory passage, we say: no.
Because the injunction (*vidhi*) must be inferred;

for, since ghee is being praised as being "essentially light" (*tejas*) in the passage "Ghee is indeed light," its status as the object of an injunction is understood, according to the maxim: "That which is praised is enjoined."
And because of that requirement, an enjoining word is inferred—namely, "anointed with ghee.
Therefore, the anointing is to be done with ghee alone.

Or rather, it is by virtue of the purpose, because it is a part of the conceptual construction; [Jaimini Sūtra 1.4.54]. (In the twentieth section concerning the determination of those things not fixed by capacity, the aphorism: [Jaimini Sūtra 1.4.55]: Or rather, it is by virtue of the purpose, because it is a part of the conceptual construction. Jaimini 1.4.30.
The twentieth section formulates the problem:

Do these [methods]—cutting with a *sruc* (ladle), with a *svadhiti* (knife), or with the hand—apply promiscuously to clarified butter (*ājya*), meat, and the *puroḍāśa* cake, or are they restricted? MJaiNy_1,4.54.
Because they lack a determining factor, the *sruc* and other implements are indeterminate;
their determination occurs through the power of the determining factor itself.
It is heard in the scripture: "He cuts with the *sruc*," "He cuts with the *svadhiti*," and "He cuts with the hand."

In that regard, if it is argued: "Regarding the sacrificial offerings consisting of clarified butter, meat, and cake (*puroḍāśa*) to be portioned out, these implements such as the *sruva* spoon and others are used interchangeably;
why?
Because there is no word [in the scripture] that establishes a fixed rule."
Not so;
for it is the capacity (*śakti*) that determines [the meaning], according to the maxim:
"When verbal roots express their meanings, capacity is the auxiliary factor."

In the cases of "he eats on a mat" (*kaṭe bhuṅkte*) and "he eats from a bronze vessel" (*kāṃsyapātryāṃ bhuṅkte*), worldly people establish a fixed rule according to the respective capacities of those objects— namely, "seated on a mat" and "having placed the rice in the bronze vessel. Likewise, in the Veda, regarding the injunction "one should offer the flour-meal with joined palms" (*añjalinā saktūn pradāya juhuyāt*), although the *añjali* is indeed the joining of both hands, [the specific application is determined by context].
Nevertheless, like the *añjali* performed for the purpose of propitiating the guru, deities, and so forth, it does not constitute a gapless union;

for in such an *añjali*, there would be no room for the barley meal (*saktu*). Therefore, by way of its functional suitability (*sāmarthya*), the *añjali* taken here consists of two joined handfuls (*prasṛti*) and possesses an intermediate space.
In the same way, here too, the *sruc* is suitable for the liquid substance, the clarified butter (*ājya*);
the specific tool, the *svadhiti*, is for the meat to be cut;
and the hand is for the solid *puroḍāśa*.
In this manner, the *sruva* ladle and the others are established.
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the first chapter in the *Jaiminīyanyāyamālāvistara* composed by the venerable Mādhava;
and the first chapter is completed.
